---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: TOCTOU race condition in `get()` causes KeyError
DESCRIPTION: The membership check `if key not in self._store` on line 19 is performed outside the lock, but the subsequent access `self._store[key]` on line 21 is inside the lock. Between the unprotected check and the lock acquisition, another thread can delete the key (via `put` eviction or `invalidate_older_than`), causing an unhandled `KeyError` that crashes the caller.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Move the `if key not in self._store` check inside the `with self._lock:` block, or use `self._store.get(key)` and check for `None`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `invalidate_older_than` reads dict values without holding lock
DESCRIPTION: On line 38, `ts, _ = self._store[key]` reads from the shared `OrderedDict` without holding `self._lock`. Concurrent `put()` or `get()` calls can mutate the dict simultaneously, leading to `KeyError`, corrupt reads, or undefined behavior in CPython's `OrderedDict` internals. Even with the GIL, the logical race means the timestamp read may not correspond to the value that is subsequently deleted.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Acquire `self._lock` once for the entire method body, protecting both the iteration and all reads/deletes.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `invalidate_older_than` can delete freshly-updated entries
DESCRIPTION: The method reads a key's timestamp outside the lock (line 38), then acquires the lock and deletes the key (line 40–41). Between the read and the delete, another thread may have called `put()` to update that key with a fresh timestamp. The stale timestamp comparison still passes, so the freshly-written entry is incorrectly evicted, causing silent data loss.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Hold a single lock for the entire method, ensuring the timestamp check and deletion are atomic.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Per-key locking in `invalidate_older_than` breaks atomicity
DESCRIPTION: The lock is acquired and released on every iteration of the loop (lines 40–42). This means other threads can interleave `put()` and `get()` calls between deletions, leaving the cache in an inconsistent intermediate state. The method's contract implies an atomic bulk eviction, but it delivers piecemeal, non-atomic deletions.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Wrap the entire for-loop in a single `with self._lock:` block.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `invalidate_older_than` KeyError when key deleted concurrently
DESCRIPTION: `list(self._store.keys())` snapshots keys on line 37, but between the snapshot and line 38's `self._store[key]` access (outside the lock), a concurrent thread can remove the key. This raises an unhandled `KeyError`, crashing the caller. The same race exists between line 38 and line 41's `del self._store[key]`.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Hold the lock for the full iteration, or guard accesses with `try/except KeyError` (the lock approach is strongly preferred).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `get()` doesn't evict expired entries on lock-miss path
DESCRIPTION: When `key not in self._store` evaluates `True` (line 19), the method returns `None` immediately. However, this check is outside the lock, so it may race with a concurrent `put`. More importantly, the "not found" path never triggers any lazy expiration scan — expired entries that are never `get()`-ed remain in the cache indefinitely, consuming memory until `invalidate_older_than` is explicitly called.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Consider a periodic or lazy background eviction strategy, or evict expired entries during `put()`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: No validation on `max_size` allows degenerate cache behavior
DESCRIPTION: If `max_size` is set to `0` or a negative value, the cache degrades silently. With `max_size=0`, every `put()` immediately evicts the entry just inserted (the `len > max_size` check is `1 > 0`). With negative values, every entry is evicted the same way. No error is raised to signal misconfiguration.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate `max_size >= 1` in `__init__` and raise `ValueError` otherwise.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: No validation on `ttl_seconds` allows instant expiration
DESCRIPTION: If `ttl_seconds` is set to `0` or a negative value, every `get()` will find `time.time() - ts > self._ttl` to be `True` and immediately delete the entry, making the cache useless. No error or warning is raised.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate `ttl_seconds > 0` in `__init__` and raise `ValueError` otherwise.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: performance
TITLE: `invalidate_older_than` is O(n) even when no entries are expired
DESCRIPTION: The method iterates over all keys every time it is called, regardless of whether any entries are actually expired. For large caches (up to 1000 entries by default, but configurable higher), this is wasteful when called frequently. The per-key lock acquisition/release compounds the overhead.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Since insertion order correlates with timestamp order (barring `move_to_end` from `get`), consider iterating from the oldest end and breaking early once a non-expired entry is found, or maintaining a separate time-sorted index.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: No metrics or logging for eviction, expiration, or cache hits/misses
DESCRIPTION: The cache provides no visibility into its behavior — no hit/miss counters, no eviction logging, no way to know the current size or expiration rate. For a component caching API responses, this makes it very difficult to diagnose performance issues, tune `max_size`/`ttl_seconds`, or detect pathological access patterns in production.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add optional hit/miss/eviction counters, or at minimum expose `__len__` so callers can monitor cache size.

---END---

raw:
# Deduplicated Code Review Findings

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: TOCTOU race condition in `get` method
DESCRIPTION: The key existence check (`if key not in self._store`) occurs outside the lock. If another thread deletes the key between the check and lock acquisition, `self._store[key]` will raise a KeyError, breaking under concurrent read/write workloads.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Move the key existence check and subsequent access inside the `with self._lock:` block to ensure atomic access.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `invalidate_older_than` acquires lock per-key and reads outside lock, causing TOCTOU and contention
DESCRIPTION: The method iterates over a snapshot of keys outside any lock, then acquires the lock only for deletion inside the loop. This creates two race conditions: (1) between snapshot and deletion, another thread may have already deleted the key, causing KeyError on `del self._store[key]`; (2) timestamp reads (`ts, _ = self._store[key]`) occur without holding the lock, exposing the method to concurrent modifications. Additionally, acquiring and releasing the lock inside the loop creates severe lock contention under high concurrency, drastically reducing throughput during bulk operations.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Acquire `self._lock` once at the method start, then iterate, read values, and delete while holding the lock throughout. This eliminates TOCTOU races and reduces lock contention.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `put` evicts entries spuriously during concurrent overwrites
DESCRIPTION: When `put` is called with an existing key at max capacity, the assignment overwrites the value without growing the store size. However, with concurrent puts racing in, the combined effect can cause spurious eviction of other valid entries due to unconditional `move_to_end` followed by the size check, leaving the cache in an inconsistent state.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Check `if key not in self._store` before the overflow guard to clearly separate new-key insertion (which may trigger eviction) from in-place updates (which should not).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: data
TITLE: System clock adjustments break TTL accuracy and entry lifetime guarantees
DESCRIPTION: Using `time.time()` for elapsed time calculations is vulnerable to NTP synchronization, manual clock changes, DST transitions, and leap seconds. Clock jumps can cause entries to expire prematurely, never expire, or appear newer than they are, corrupting cache consistency across distributed or long-running processes.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace all `time.time()` calls with `time.monotonic()` to guarantee monotonically increasing time measurements.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `get` does not update LRU order when deleting expired entries
DESCRIPTION: When `put` inserts a new entry exceeding `max_size`, `popitem(last=False)` correctly evicts the LRU item. However, `get` silently deletes expired entries without updating LRU ordering, potentially leaving stale entries that still count against `max_size`, degrading cache effectiveness.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Delete expired entries immediately upon detection and update LRU ordering, or document that expired entries consume capacity until explicitly accessed or invalidated.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Zero or negative `max_size` causes perpetual cache emptiness
DESCRIPTION: If `max_size <= 0`, every `put` call will immediately evict the entry it just inserted (since `len > 0` is immediately true), leaving the cache permanently empty. There is no validation in `__init__`.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add `if max_size < 1: raise ValueError("max_size must be >= 1")` in `__init__`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Negative or zero `ttl_seconds` makes all entries immediately expired
DESCRIPTION: A `ttl_seconds` of `0` or negative means `time.time() - ts > self._ttl` is always true immediately after insertion, so every `get` will return `None` and delete the entry, wasting CPU cycles on constant cache thrashing. There is no guard in `__init__`.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add `if ttl_seconds <= 0: raise ValueError("ttl_seconds must be positive")` in `__init__`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: `invalidate_older_than` with `age_seconds <= 0` wipes entire cache
DESCRIPTION: If `age_seconds <= 0`, the cutoff equals or exceeds `time.time()`, so every entry's timestamp will be less than the cutoff and the entire cache will be cleared. This surprising behavior is undocumented with no safeguard.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Document this behavior explicitly, or add a guard: `if age_seconds <= 0: raise ValueError("age_seconds must be positive")`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Expired entries accumulate and bypass `max_size` capacity limit
DESCRIPTION: TTL validation only occurs lazily on `get`. If a key is never accessed again after expiry, the stale entry remains in `_store` indefinitely and counts against `max_size`, potentially evicting live entries and defeating the intended capacity guarantee.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement periodic background eviction with a sweeper thread, validate TTL during `put` to filter stale entries, or document this limitation as a behavioral caveat.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: No cache hit/miss/eviction metrics or logging
DESCRIPTION: For a cache serving API responses, there is no instrumentation for hit rate, miss rate, TTL evictions, LRU evictions, or current size. Without this, diagnosing cache effectiveness, capacity planning, and production performance regressions is impossible.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add counters (e.g., `self._hits`, `self._misses`, `self._lru_evictions`, `self._ttl_evictions`) updated atomically under the lock, and expose them via a `stats()` method or standard metrics interface.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Absolute TTL does not refresh on cache hits
DESCRIPTION: The `get` method updates the LRU order on successful hits but does not reset the entry's timestamp. This results in absolute expiration rather than sliding TTL, which may not match expected API caching behavior where hits extend the lifetime.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Update the timestamp tuple on successful hits if sliding TTL is desired, or document the absolute TTL behavior clearly.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `get` returns `None` ambiguously for missing vs. expired entries
DESCRIPTION: Both a cache miss and a TTL expiry return `None`, making it impossible for the caller to distinguish between "key was never set" and "key existed but expired." This can lead to incorrect retry or fallback logic in callers.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Return a sentinel object, raise a distinct exception, or document the ambiguity explicitly and require callers to handle it.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Unbounded object storage enables memory exhaustion
DESCRIPTION: The cache stores arbitrary Python objects without size limits or type restrictions. Malicious or large payloads can be injected via `put`, enabling uncontrolled memory growth and potential denial of service attacks.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement a maximum entry size limit, validate object types or sizes before insertion, or use a serialization layer to enforce memory bounds.

---END---

findings.suggested_fix: Add `if max_size < 1: raise ValueError("max_size must be >= 1")` in `__init__`.

Oto zsynthezyzowana lista deduplikowanych ustaleń:

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Race Condition in `get()` — Check Outside Lock
DESCRIPTION: The `get()` method checks `if key not in self._store:` before acquiring the lock. Another thread can delete, insert, or replace the entry between this unprotected check and the subsequent locked access, causing a `KeyError` on the `self._store[key]` line or returning stale/inconsistent data. When the staleness check happens inside the lock but the membership test is outside, concurrent `put()` calls can interleave, causing `get()` to read stale or incorrect data if an entry is deleted and re-inserted by another thread. This defeats the purpose of locking entirely for the read path.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Move the `if key not in self._store` check inside the `with self._lock:` block so membership test and read are atomic. Perform all reads and writes under a single lock acquisition in `get()`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Non-Atomic Locking in `invalidate_older_than()` — Lock Per-Iteration
DESCRIPTION: The method iterates over `list(self._store.keys())` and reads entries outside the lock, only acquiring it per-key for deletion. This breaks atomicity multiple ways: (1) Between snapshotting keys and accessing entries, concurrent threads may delete/replace keys, causing `KeyError`; (2) Per-key lock acquire/release allows concurrent `put()`/`get()` operations to interleave mid-scan, leaving the dict inconsistent; (3) Returned removal count becomes unreliable — items may be double-counted, skipped, or create races where concurrent calls try to delete the same key (second raises `KeyError`); (4) Excessive lock contention. Concurrent calls to `invalidate_older_than()` or concurrent `get()` operations (which also delete expired entries) can fail with `KeyError`.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Acquire the lock once at the top of the method before iteration, perform all deletions inside a single lock acquisition, then release. Alternatively, use `self._store.pop(key, None)` instead of `del self._store[key]`, or hold the lock for the entire operation to ensure atomic state inspection and modification.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Clock Drift Causes Unreliable TTL Expiration
DESCRIPTION: The code uses `time.time()` for TTL calculations, which can jump backwards due to NTP adjustments or manual system clock changes. When the system clock jumps backward, existing cached entries may be considered expired immediately. When the clock jumps forward, expired entries may never expire, breaking cache consistency guarantees and potentially serving stale data indefinitely.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace all `time.time()` calls with `time.monotonic()` for reliable, monotonic time tracking independent of system clock adjustments.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Missing Input Validation for Cache Parameters
DESCRIPTION: `__init__` accepts negative or zero values for `max_size` and `ttl_seconds` without validation. When `max_size <= 0`, the cache either refuses to store any entries or exhibits undefined behavior. When `ttl_seconds <= 0`, every `get()` call finds all entries expired, making the cache non-functional. These invalid parameters are silently accepted, leading to silent cache failure in production.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add validation in `__init__` to raise `ValueError` if `max_size <= 0` or `ttl_seconds <= 0`, rejecting all non-positive inputs.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: No Eviction of Expired Entries During `put()`
DESCRIPTION: When the cache is full and a new entry must be added, `put()` evicts the least-recently-used entry, which may still be valid. However, many expired entries could remain in the cache consuming space. The effective cache capacity is reduced by these expired entries, which are only cleaned up lazily on `get()` or explicit `invalidate_older_than()` calls. This violates expected TTL cache semantics where expired entries should not consume space.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Before checking size and evicting LRU entries, optionally purge expired entries first. Alternatively, evict expired entries preferentially over valid LRU entries when capacity is reached.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: TTL Not Reset on Cache Access
DESCRIPTION: The `get()` method updates the LRU order via `move_to_end` when retrieving an entry, but does not update the stored timestamp. Entries expire based on creation time regardless of access frequency, which contradicts standard TTL-on-access cache behavior where frequently-accessed entries should have their TTL renewed.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Update the timestamp tuple in `_store` when `get()` successfully retrieves a non-expired entry, or document that TTL is strictly creation-time based, not access-time based.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: Memory Spike and Performance Issues from Key Snapshot Creation
DESCRIPTION: `invalidate_older_than()` calls `list(self._store.keys())`, creating a full in-memory copy of all cache keys. For large caches, this doubles memory usage temporarily and can trigger garbage collection pauses or OOM conditions. Additionally, the method always performs a full scan instead of stopping early; while OrderedDict is ordered by insertion/access, `move_to_end` on `get()` disrupts timestamp ordering so early termination is unreliable. The O(n) cost is not documented and can be wasteful for large caches.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Iterate directly over `self._store.items()` or use a generator to avoid materializing the entire key list in memory. Document the O(n) cost, or break early if strict LRU ordering is acceptable as a proxy for age.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: LRU Order Inconsistency After Bulk Removal
DESCRIPTION: `invalidate_older_than()` removes old entries but leaves remaining items in original insertion order, breaking strict LRU semantics. This can cause unexpected eviction patterns when the cache reaches capacity.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Rebuild the LRU order by moving remaining items to the end, or document that bulk removals do not preserve LRU ordering.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Ambiguous TTL Semantics in Method Documentation
DESCRIPTION: The method name `invalidate_older_than` and implementation compare against creation time (`ts`), but TTL caches often imply expiration based on last access. This ambiguity can mislead consumers expecting access-time-based expiration rather than insertion-time-based.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Rename to `invalidate_older_than_creation` for clarity, or explicitly document that age is measured from insertion time, not last access.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Unhandled Negative Age Parameter in `invalidate_older_than()`
DESCRIPTION: `invalidate_older_than()` accepts negative `age_seconds` without validation. Negative values result in a cutoff time in the future, causing zero removals and silently masking caller errors.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate `age_seconds` at method start and raise `ValueError` for negative inputs, or clamp to zero.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: No Metrics or Logging for Cache Behavior
DESCRIPTION: The cache provides no visibility into hit/miss rates, eviction counts, or expired-entry removal counts. Operators cannot tune `max_size` or `ttl_seconds` or debug cache issues without external instrumentation.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add counters for cache hits, misses, LRU evictions, TTL evictions, and expose them via a `stats()` method or configurable logging.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: data
TITLE: Loss of Type Information in Return Type
DESCRIPTION: `get()` returns `object | None`, providing no type safety. Callers must cast or assert on every retrieval, increasing runtime type error risk and reducing IDE autocomplete quality.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Make `TTLCache` generic using `typing.Generic[T]` so callers get properly typed return values from `get()`.

Oto zsyntezowana, zdeduplikowana lista ustaleń z raportów trzech recenzentów:

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: TOCTOU race condition in get() - membership check outside lock
DESCRIPTION: The `if key not in self._store` check executes without holding `self._lock`. A concurrent call to `put()` (via eviction), `invalidate_older_than()`, or other deletion can remove the key between this unsynchronized check and the subsequent locked `self._store[key]` access, raising `KeyError` and crashing the caller. Additionally, a concurrent `put()` could insert the key after the false check, and the caller incorrectly receives `None` instead of the value.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Move the entire body of `get()` inside `with self._lock`, using `self._store.get(key)` or wrapping `self._store[key]` in try/except to safely handle concurrent deletions.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: invalidate_older_than() reads and iterates dictionary without lock
DESCRIPTION: The `list(self._store.keys())` and `ts, _ = self._store[key]` operations execute without holding the lock. A concurrent `put()` eviction or another `invalidate_older_than()` call can delete a key between the snapshot and the read, raising `KeyError`. Additionally, the `list()` snapshot of `OrderedDict.keys()` is not atomic with respect to concurrent structural modifications, which can corrupt internal state in CPython.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Wrap the entire method body in `with self._lock`, reading and building a list of expired keys before deleting them, ensuring atomicity.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Improper lock scope in invalidate_older_than() - per-key locking causes TOCTOU and non-atomicity
DESCRIPTION: The lock is acquired and released once per key deletion, not once for the entire operation. This creates two problems: (1) between iterations, other threads can `put()` or `get()` entries, interleaving with the eviction sweep and making the purge non-atomic, (2) a race exists between the `if ts < cutoff` check (outside the lock) and the `del self._store[key]` (inside the lock), allowing another thread to delete the same key, causing `KeyError` inside the critical section.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Acquire the lock once before iterating, collect all expired keys, and delete them all within a single critical section to ensure atomicity and prevent TOCTOU races.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Missing validation of constructor parameters (max_size and ttl_seconds)
DESCRIPTION: The constructor does not validate `max_size` or `ttl_seconds`. If `max_size` is zero or negative, every `put()` inserts an entry then immediately evicts it, resulting in a permanently empty cache. If `ttl_seconds` is zero or negative, every `get()` treats every entry as expired and deletes it, breaking cache functionality. Both cases produce silent, hard-to-diagnose misbehavior in production.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate in `__init__` that `max_size >= 1` and `ttl_seconds > 0`, raising `ValueError` if invalid.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: time.time() is not monotonic - TTL breaks on clock adjustments
DESCRIPTION: The code uses `time.time()` for TTL tracking, which reflects wall-clock time. System clock adjustments (NTP step, DST, manual adjustment) can cause the clock to jump backward or forward. A backward jump makes insertion timestamps appear newer than "now," effectively making entries immortal. A forward jump instantly expires valid entries, causing unexpected cache misses.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `time.monotonic()` for all timestamp comparisons and TTL calculations, as it is immune to system clock adjustments and always moves forward.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: get() returns direct reference to mutable cached objects
DESCRIPTION: The method returns the raw value from the cache without copying. If the cached object is mutable (list, dict, object), external code can modify it, and the cache has no way to track the change. This breaks cache consistency and can cause subtle data corruption bugs where code assumes cached data is stable.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Return a deep copy of the value, or explicitly document that callers must treat returned objects as immutable.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: performance
TITLE: Inefficient memory allocation in invalidate_older_than()
DESCRIPTION: The method calls `list(self._store.keys())` to create a complete snapshot of all keys before iteration. This unnecessarily duplicates memory usage proportional to the cache size, causing significant memory pressure in large caches.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Iterate directly over `self._store.items()` (once synchronization is fixed), or collect keys to delete in a temporary list without pre-allocating the full key snapshot.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: performance
TITLE: O(n) scan in invalidate_older_than() - lacks early termination
DESCRIPTION: Because `move_to_end` in `get()` reorders entries by access recency (LRU), insertion-order does not match expiration-time order. This forces a full scan of all entries, even if only a few are expired. For large caches, this is an unnecessary O(n) operation that holds the lock (once fixed) for the entire traversal, blocking all other cache operations.
SUGGESTED_FIX: If time-ordered eviction is frequent, maintain a secondary min-heap or time-sorted index by insertion timestamp for early termination. Otherwise, prioritize the critical synchronization fixes.

---END---

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: TOCTOU race condition in get() key check
DESCRIPTION: The `if key not in self._store:` check occurs outside the lock. Another thread can delete or modify the entry between the check and the lock acquisition, leading to a KeyError or inconsistent state when the lock is finally acquired.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Move the key existence check inside the `with self._lock:` block, or remove it and handle KeyError/expiration directly within the lock.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Inconsistent lock acquisition in invalidate_older_than()
DESCRIPTION: The method acquires and releases the lock inside the loop for each deletion. This causes unnecessary contention and leaves the cache in a partially updated state between iterations if another thread modifies it concurrently.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Acquire the lock once at the start of the method, perform all deletions, and release it before returning.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Unbounded growth when max_size is zero or negative
DESCRIPTION: The condition `if len(self._store) > self._max_size:` never triggers if `max_size <= 0`, causing the cache to grow without bound and eventually exhaust memory.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add a validation check in `__init__` to raise `ValueError` if `max_size <= 0`, or handle it by immediately evicting or rejecting inserts.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Expired entries inflate cache size beyond max_size
DESCRIPTION: `put()` checks `len(self._store)` against `max_size`, but expired entries are only removed lazily in `get()`. The cache can grow indefinitely past `max_size` if new keys are inserted while old ones sit expired.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement periodic background eviction or check expiration count during `put()`, or document that `max_size` applies to total entries, not just live ones.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Non-reentrant lock risks deadlock on nested calls
DESCRIPTION: `threading.Lock()` is not reentrant. If any method calls another method that also acquires the lock (e.g., `get()` calling `put()` or vice versa), it will deadlock.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `threading.RLock()` instead of `threading.Lock()` to allow safe nested locking within the same thread.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Clock drift vulnerability using time.time() for TTL
DESCRIPTION: `time.time()` can jump backwards due to NTP adjustments or system clock changes, causing TTL calculations to behave unpredictably or entries to expire prematurely or never.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace `time.time()` with `time.monotonic()` for all timestamp comparisons to ensure strictly increasing time values.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: performance
TITLE: Redundant move_to_end() call in put()
DESCRIPTION: Assigning a value to an existing key in `OrderedDict` automatically moves it to the end in modern Python versions. The explicit call is unnecessary and adds minor overhead.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Remove `self._store.move_to_end(key)` from `put()` as it is redundant.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Negative or zero TTL causes immediate expiration
DESCRIPTION: If `ttl_seconds` is passed as 0 or negative, `time.time() - ts > self._ttl` will immediately evaluate to True, causing all entries to be deleted upon retrieval.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate `ttl_seconds > 0` in `__init__` and raise `ValueError` for invalid inputs.

---END---

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `get` checks key existence outside the lock
DESCRIPTION: `if key not in self._store:` runs before acquiring `self._lock`, creating a TOCTOU race. Another thread can delete the key between the check and the `with self._lock:` block, causing a `KeyError` inside the lock on the `self._store[key]` access.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Move the `key not in self._store` check inside the `with self._lock:` block, or use `self._store.get(key)` inside the lock.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `invalidate_older_than` acquires lock per-key, not once
DESCRIPTION: The loop iterates outside any lock and acquires `self._lock` only for the `del` operation. Between reading `self._store[key]` and entering the lock, another thread may have already deleted that key, causing a `KeyError`. Additionally, the unprotected `for key in list(self._store.keys())` snapshot is stale by the time deletions happen, and interleaved `put` calls can corrupt LRU order.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Acquire `self._lock` once for the entire method body, build the list of keys to delete inside the lock, then delete them all before releasing.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `invalidate_older_than` reads store entries without holding the lock
DESCRIPTION: `ts, _ = self._store[key]` is executed outside `self._lock`. A concurrent `put` or eviction can delete or replace that key between the loop's key snapshot and this read, raising a `KeyError` or reading a stale timestamp from a newly inserted entry with the same key.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Hold `self._lock` for the full duration of `invalidate_older_than`, not just around the `del`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `put` does not overwrite TTL on existing key update
DESCRIPTION: When an existing key is updated via `put`, `move_to_end` is called after assignment, which is correct for LRU order, but the timestamp is refreshed correctly. However, if a key already exists, it is moved to the end after being written, which is fine. The real issue: `put` does not evict the *least recently used* item correctly when `max_size` is exceeded after an update to an existing key — the store size does not grow, so `popitem(last=False)` evicts a valid entry unnecessarily. The size check should be conditioned on whether the key is new.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Check `if key not in self._store` before deciding whether to evict; only evict when a new key is being inserted and `len(self._store) >= self._max_size`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: TTL expiry uses `>` instead of `>=`, off-by-one at boundary
DESCRIPTION: `if time.time() - ts > self._ttl` means an entry whose age is exactly `ttl_seconds` is still considered valid. The TTL contract ("expire after N seconds") is violated at the exact boundary, which can cause stale data to be returned.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Change `>` to `>=` so entries at or beyond TTL are evicted.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `put` does not check for expired entry before inserting
DESCRIPTION: When inserting a key that already exists but is expired, `put` overwrites the value correctly, but the old expired entry's slot is reused without any TTL-based eviction pass. The size check then runs, potentially evicting a *fresh* LRU entry while the cache already held a logically expired (but not yet removed) entry, wasting a slot.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Inside `put`, after acquiring the lock, check if the existing key is expired and remove it before re-inserting to keep accounting consistent.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: `max_size=0` causes infinite eviction loop or immediate eviction
DESCRIPTION: If `max_size` is set to `0`, every `put` call will trigger `popitem(last=False)` because `len(self._store) > 0` is immediately true after insertion. The item just inserted is evicted on every write, making the cache non-functional with no error or warning.

SEVERITY: medium

SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: edge-case

findings.title: `get` checks key existence outside the lock
findings.description: `if key not in self._store:` runs before acquiring `self._lock`, creating a TOCTOU race. Another thread can delete the key between the check and the `with self._lock:` block, causing a `KeyError` inside the lock on the `self._store[key]` access.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the `key not in self._store` check inside the `with self._lock:` block, or use `self._store.get(key)` inside the lock.

findings.title: `invalidate_older_than` acquires lock per-key, not once
findings.description: The loop iterates outside any lock and acquires `self._lock` only for the `del` operation. Between reading `self._store[key]` and entering the lock, another thread may have already deleted that key, causing a `KeyError`. Additionally, the unprotected `for key in list(self._store.keys())` snapshot is stale by the time deletions happen, and interleaved `put` calls can corrupt LRU order.
findings.suggested_fix: Acquire `self._lock` once for the entire method body, build the list of keys to delete inside the lock, then delete them all before releasing.

findings.title: `put` does not overwrite TTL on existing key update
findings.description: When an existing key is updated via `put`, `move_to_end` is called after assignment, which is correct for LRU order, but the timestamp is refreshed correctly. However, if a key already exists, it is moved to the end after being written, which is fine. The real issue: `put` does not evict the *least recently used* item correctly when `max_size` is exceeded after an update to an existing key — the store size does not grow, so `popitem(last=False)` evicts a valid entry unnecessarily. The size check should be conditioned on whether the key is new.
findings.suggested_fix: Check `if key not in self._store` before deciding whether to evict; only evict when a new key is being inserted and `len(self._store) >= self._max_size`.

findings.title: TTL expiry uses `>` instead of `>=`, off-by-one at boundary

findings.suggested_fix: Change `>` to `>=` so entries at or beyond TTL are evicted.

findings.title: `put` does not check for expired entry before inserting

The size check then runs, potentially evicting a *fresh* LRU entry while the cache already held a logically expired (but not yet removed) entry, wasting a slot.

raw:
---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: MD5 used for password hashing
DESCRIPTION: `hash_password` uses `hashlib.md5`, which is cryptographically broken and extremely fast to brute-force. Modern GPUs can compute billions of MD5 hashes per second, making rainbow table and dictionary attacks trivial. This applies to every user whose password is stored via this function.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace with a purpose-built password hashing algorithm such as `bcrypt`, `argon2`, or `hashlib.scrypt` with appropriate cost parameters.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Session token exposed in URL query parameters
DESCRIPTION: `create_session` places the session token in the redirect URL's query string. Query parameters are logged by web servers, proxies, CDNs, and browser history, and are visible in the `Referer` header when the user navigates away. This makes session hijacking significantly easier.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Transmit the session token via a `Set-Cookie` header with `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, and `SameSite` attributes, or pass it in a POST body or `Authorization` header instead of the URL.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: User ID leaked in redirect URL query parameters
DESCRIPTION: The `uid` parameter is included in the callback URL alongside the session token. This unnecessarily exposes internal user identifiers to the browser, logs, and any intermediary. It provides no functional value since the server can already resolve the user from the session token via `SESSIONS[token]`.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Remove the `uid` parameter from the redirect URL. Look up the user ID server-side from the session token.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Open redirect via unvalidated `redirect_url`
DESCRIPTION: `create_session` embeds the caller-supplied `redirect_url` directly into the callback URL without validation. An attacker can craft a login link with `redirect_url=https://evil.com`, and after successful authentication the user is redirected to a phishing site while believing they are interacting with the legitimate application.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate `redirect_url` against an allowlist of permitted domains/paths before including it in the response.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Password hash comparison vulnerable to timing attack
DESCRIPTION: The `==` operator in `login` performs a byte-by-byte string comparison that short-circuits on the first mismatch. An attacker can statistically measure response times to deduce the stored hash character by character, eventually reconstructing it.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `hmac.compare_digest(hash_password(password, salt), stored_hash)` for constant-time comparison.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: No session expiration or invalidation mechanism
DESCRIPTION: Tokens added to `SESSIONS` are never removed or expired. Once created, a session token remains valid indefinitely. If a token is leaked or a user logs out, there is no way to revoke access. In the in-memory implementation this resets on restart, but the stated production backend is Redis, where keys persist.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add a TTL to each session (e.g., Redis `SETEX`) and provide an explicit `logout` / `revoke_session` function that deletes the token.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: In-memory `SESSIONS` dict is not thread-safe
DESCRIPTION: The global `SESSIONS` dictionary is accessed from `create_session` and `verify_session` without synchronization. Under a multi-threaded WSGI server (e.g., gunicorn with thread workers), concurrent writes can cause lost updates or corruption of the dict's internal state in CPython versions where dict operations are not guaranteed atomic for all mutation patterns.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a `threading.Lock` to protect access, or rely exclusively on the Redis backend in production with atomic `SET`/`GET` operations.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Single unsalted MD5 iteration — no key stretching
DESCRIPTION: Even if a stronger algorithm were used, the function performs only a single hash iteration with simple string concatenation of password and salt. There is no key stretching (iterations/cost factor), so the hash is as fast to attack as the raw algorithm permits. The concatenation order (`password + salt`) is also susceptible to certain preimage constructions compared to HMAC-based mixing.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a KDF with a configurable work factor (`bcrypt`, `argon2id`, or `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac` with ≥600,000 iterations).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: No brute-force or rate-limiting protection on login
DESCRIPTION: The `login` function performs a single hash comparison with no throttling, lockout, or rate limiting. An attacker can invoke it at high speed to brute-force passwords, especially given the fast MD5 hash function.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement rate limiting (e.g., per-IP or per-user-id exponential backoff) and account lockout after repeated failures.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: No input validation on `user_id` or `password`
DESCRIPTION: `create_session` and `hash_password` accept arbitrary strings without checking for empty, excessively long, or null-byte-containing values. An empty `user_id` would create a valid session for a meaningless identity; an extremely long password could cause performance issues in the hash function.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate that `user_id` is non-empty and within expected bounds, and enforce a reasonable maximum length on `password`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: No logging of authentication events
DESCRIPTION: Neither successful logins nor failed attempts are logged. This makes it impossible to detect brute-force attacks, compromised accounts, or suspicious login patterns during incident response or forensic analysis.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Log authentication successes and failures with timestamp, user ID, and source IP (but never the password or full token).

---END---

raw:
Oto zsyntezowana lista deduplikowanych ustaleń z obu recenzentów:

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Cryptographically broken MD5 used for password hashing
DESCRIPTION: The `hash_password` function relies on `hashlib.md5`, which is not a password hashing function. MD5 is extremely fast and has no work-factor tuning, enabling billions of guesses per second on commodity hardware. It is trivially reversible via rainbow tables and brute force, completely undermining authentication security.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace MD5 with a dedicated password hashing library like `bcrypt`, `argon2-cffi`, or at minimum `hashlib.scrypt`/`hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac` with a high iteration count. Never implement a custom password hashing scheme.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Session token exposed in redirect URL query string
DESCRIPTION: `create_session` embeds the session token directly in the URL as `?session=<token>`. URLs appear in browser history, server access logs, proxy logs, and the `Referer` header on any subsequent navigation. This makes the session token trivially harvestable from logs or history, leading to full account takeover.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Set the session token as an `HttpOnly`/`Secure` cookie in the HTTP response instead of embedding it in a URL query parameter; never transmit a bearer token in a URL.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Unvalidated redirect URL enables open redirect attacks
DESCRIPTION: The `redirect_url` parameter is passed directly into the query string without validation or allowlisting. An attacker can craft a malicious URL that redirects users to a phishing site after authentication, bypassing security controls.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate `redirect_url` against a strict allowlist of trusted domains or use a relative path/internal routing mechanism before including it in the callback.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: User ID exposed in callback URL parameters
DESCRIPTION: The `uid` parameter is included in the generated redirect URL, unnecessarily exposing the internal user identifier to the client and potential log files (browser history, logs, referrer headers). This can leak PII and aid attackers in mapping user accounts. Combined with the exposed session token, this doubles the information exposure surface.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Remove `uid` from the URL parameters and rely solely on the server-side session token to look up the authenticated user's identity.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Timing attack vulnerability in hash comparison
DESCRIPTION: The `login` function uses the `==` operator to compare the computed password hash against the stored hash. This performs a byte-by-byte comparison that leaks timing information, allowing attackers to brute-force the hash character by character or infer characters of the stored hash.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `hmac.compare_digest()` or `secrets.compare_digest()` for constant-time comparison of cryptographic hashes to prevent timing side-channel attacks.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Global mutable `SESSIONS` dict causes race conditions
DESCRIPTION: `SESSIONS` is a module-level dictionary accessed concurrently by multiple threads or processes. Simultaneous reads and writes are not protected by any lock. Python's GIL offers limited protection for individual bytecode ops but does not guarantee atomicity across the read-modify-write operations in `create_session` and `verify_session`, leading to lost updates, corrupted state, or inconsistent session lookups in production environments.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Wrap accesses with a `threading.Lock`, or replace the dict with a thread-safe session store like Redis for production use.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Sessions lack expiration or timeout mechanisms
DESCRIPTION: Tokens stored in `SESSIONS` never expire, meaning compromised session tokens remain valid indefinitely. There is no TTL, no logout path, and no way to revoke a compromised token. A leaked token grants permanent access, violating security best practices and increasing the window of opportunity for session hijacking attacks.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Store a creation timestamp alongside each session and reject tokens older than a configurable TTL in `verify_session`; add a `delete_session(token)` function for logout.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Salt is caller-supplied with no proper generation or validation
DESCRIPTION: `hash_password` accepts an externally provided `salt`. If the caller passes an empty string, a static string, or reuses salts across users, the protection against rainbow tables is voided. There is no enforcement that salts are unique per user or meet a minimum length.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Generate the salt internally using `secrets.token_bytes(16)` inside `hash_password` (or the caller's registration path) and store it alongside the hash; never trust an externally supplied salt.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Session token entropy is minimal (128 bits) with no security margin
DESCRIPTION: `secrets.token_hex(16)` produces 128 bits, which is the absolute minimum recommended by NIST for session tokens. While currently adequate, this leaves no security margin if the RNG assumption is weakened or the token is shortened elsewhere.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Increase to `secrets.token_hex(32)` (256 bits) to provide a comfortable security margin with negligible cost.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: No rate limiting or account lockout on `login`
DESCRIPTION: `login` performs a hash comparison on every call with no throttling, lockout, or CAPTCHA. An attacker can perform an unbounded brute-force attack directly against this function. MD5's computational speed makes this especially severe.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement rate limiting per `user_id`/IP (e.g., with a token-bucket counter in Redis) and lock the account after a configurable number of consecutive failures.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: Unbounded session dictionary causes memory leaks
DESCRIPTION: The `SESSIONS` dictionary grows indefinitely as new tokens are created but never cleaned up. Over time, this will consume unbounded memory, eventually causing application crashes or degraded performance in long-running processes.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Evict expired sessions eagerly on writes or lazily on reads, implement a background cleanup task, or use a session store with automatic eviction policies (e.g., Redis with `EXPIRE`).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `login` function mixes authentication and session management
DESCRIPTION: The `login` function handles both credential verification and session creation, violating the single responsibility principle. This makes the function harder to test, reuse, and maintain, especially if authentication logic changes.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Split the function into `authenticate_user()` for credential verification and `create_session()` for token generation, allowing independent testing and composition.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: `verify_session` lacks token format and state validation
DESCRIPTION: The function blindly returns the stored `user_id` without validating the token's format, checking for revocation, or ensuring the session hasn't been invalidated. Malformed or revoked tokens could be accepted.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add validation checks for token format, revocation status, and expiration before returning the associated `user_id`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Missing input validation on function parameters
DESCRIPTION: Functions accept `user_id`, `password`, `token`, and `redirect_url` without validating their format, type, or length. A caller passing `None`, an empty string, or a multi-megabyte string will cause silent misbehavior, downstream parsing errors, or injection vulnerabilities.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add explicit type checking at function entry, reject empty strings, enforce reasonable maximum lengths, and validate format constraints before using inputs.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: `redirect_url` could enable Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
DESCRIPTION: If the returned URL is ever followed server-side (e.g., the application fetches the redirect target to validate it), an attacker supplying an internal address (`http://169.254.169.254/`, `http://internal-service/`) could trigger SSRF. The current code does not make the request, but the pattern sets up the vulnerability for any downstream code that does.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate and allowlist `redirect_url` before use (as recommended in the open-redirect finding); this also mitigates SSRF.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `create_session` overwrites existing token on collision without notice
DESCRIPTION: If `token` collides with an existing key in `SESSIONS` (astronomically rare but theoretically possible), the existing user's session is silently overwritten. No collision detection or regeneration loop exists.
SUGGESTED_FIX: After generating the token, check `if token in SESSIONS` and regenerate; log a warning if a collision occurs, as it may indicate RNG issues.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: No logging of authentication events
DESCRIPTION: Neither successful logins nor failures are logged. This makes forensic analysis, anomaly detection, and audit trails impossible. Failed login attempts in particular are a key signal for detecting brute-force attacks.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add structured log lines (using the `logging` module) for login success, login failure (without including the password), and session creation, including timestamp and user identifier.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Password concatenated with salt without proper encoding
DESCRIPTION: `(password + salt).encode()` concatenates in a fixed order with no separator. If password or salt contains overlapping byte sequences, two different (password, salt) pairs could produce the same input to MD5 (e.g., password=`ab`, salt=`c` vs password=`a`, salt=`bc`), creating a pre-image ambiguity.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a structured format with a separator, or use a proper HMAC/KDF that accepts key and data separately; this issue is moot if you switch to bcrypt/argon2 as recommended.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: `urlencode` may double-encode pre-encoded redirect URLs
DESCRIPTION: If `redirect_url` is already URL-encoded, `urlencode` will encode special characters again, potentially breaking the redirect target or causing authentication failures on the callback endpoint.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Ensure `redirect_url` is passed as a raw string to `urlencode`, or verify that inputs are not pre-encoded before processing.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: configuration
TITLE: Hardcoded callback hostname makes code environment-unaware
DESCRIPTION: The base URL `https://app.example.com/callback` is hardcoded in `create_session`. In real deployments this must vary per environment; hardcoding it forces callers to post-process the returned URL.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Accept the base callback URL as a parameter or read it from application configuration.

---END---

CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Password concatenated with salt without proper encoding
DESCRIPTION: `(password + salt).encode()` concatenates in a fixed order with no separator. If password or salt contains overlapping byte sequences, two different (password, salt) pairs could produce the same input to MD5 (e.g., password=`ab`, salt=`c` vs password=`a`, salt=`bc`), creating a pre-image ambiguity.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a structured format with a separator, or use a proper HMAC/KDF that accepts key and data separately; this issue is moot if you switch to bcrypt/argon2 as recommended.

findings.title: `urlencode` may double-encode pre-encoded redirect URLs
findings.description: If `redirect_url` is already URL-encoded, `urlencode` will encode special characters again, potentially breaking the redirect target or causing authentication failures on the callback endpoint.
findings.suggested_fix: Ensure `redirect_url` is passed as a raw string to `urlencode`, or verify that inputs are not pre-encoded before processing.

findings.suggested_fix: Accept the base callback URL as a parameter or read it from application configuration.

raw:
Syntetuję i deduplikuję wyniki z 3 niezależnych recenzentów. Oto skonsolidowana lista znalezisk:

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: MD5 used for password hashing
DESCRIPTION: The `hash_password` function relies on MD5, which is cryptographically broken and far too fast for password hashing. MD5 is vulnerable to collision and preimage attacks, and an attacker with a leaked database can brute-force billions of hashes per second on commodity GPUs, rendering salting nearly useless. This completely fails modern compliance and security standards.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace MD5 with a purpose-built password hashing algorithm such as `bcrypt`, `scrypt`, or `argon2id` (via the `argon2-cffi` library), all of which include built-in salting and configurable work factors.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Open redirect via unvalidated redirect_url parameter
DESCRIPTION: The `create_session` function accepts a caller-supplied `redirect_url` and embeds it directly into the callback URL without any validation or allowlist check. An attacker can craft a login link with a malicious `redirect_url` pointing to a phishing site, and after successful authentication, the user will be seamlessly redirected to the attacker's domain, where their session token can be stolen or they can be socially engineered.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate the `redirect_url` against a strict whitelist of allowed domains or paths before including it in the redirect. Reject any URL pointing to an external origin.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Timing attack vulnerability in password hash comparison
DESCRIPTION: The `login` function compares the computed hash against the stored hash using the `==` operator, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. An attacker can statistically measure response times across many requests to deduce the correct hash one character at a time, especially in network-accessible scenarios.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `hmac.compare_digest()` or `secrets.compare_digest()` for constant-time string comparison to prevent timing side-channel attacks.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Session token exposed in URL query parameters
DESCRIPTION: The session token is embedded in the redirect URL as a query parameter (`?session=...`). Query strings are recorded in browser history, server access logs, proxy logs, and transmitted in `Referer` headers when users navigate away. Any of these leakage paths allows attackers to hijack sessions.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Transmit the session token via a secure, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite` cookie or through a short-lived authorization code that is exchanged server-side, rather than exposing it in the query string.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Sessions never expire
DESCRIPTION: Once created, a session token persists in the `SESSIONS` dictionary indefinitely with no TTL, expiration timestamp, or cleanup mechanism. Stolen or leaked tokens remain valid forever, maximizing the window for session hijacking and violating security best practices.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Store a creation timestamp alongside each session token and enforce a maximum session lifetime (e.g., 30 minutes). Evict expired entries on access or via a periodic sweep. In production, use Redis with TTL support.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Global SESSIONS dictionary is not thread-safe and not suitable for multi-process deployments
DESCRIPTION: The `SESSIONS` dictionary is a global mutable object accessed without synchronization primitives. In multi-threaded servers, concurrent requests can cause race conditions and data corruption. In typical production deployments (multiple worker processes or container replicas), a session created in one process is invisible to others, causing spurious authentication failures.
SUGGESTED_FIX: For thread-safety, protect access with a `threading.Lock`. For production multi-process deployments, migrate to a proper shared session store like Redis or a database that provides atomic operations and horizontal scalability.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: User ID exposed in redirect URL
DESCRIPTION: The `create_session` function includes the `user_id` directly in the callback URL's query parameters as `uid`. This exposes internal identifiers to the client, browser history, server logs, and referrer headers, enabling user enumeration attacks and allowing adversaries to target specific users.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Remove the `uid` parameter from the callback URL. The server can look up the user ID from the session token via `verify_session` when the callback is processed.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Login endpoint lacks brute-force protection
DESCRIPTION: The `login` function accepts unlimited authentication attempts without any rate limiting, account lockout, or exponential backoff mechanisms. An attacker can make unlimited password guesses at machine speed, especially dangerous given the weak MD5 hashing algorithm.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement rate limiting on the login endpoint (per user ID and per source IP, e.g., via token bucket or sliding-window counter) and consider temporary account lockout or CAPTCHA after a threshold of failed attempts.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: In-memory session storage causes unbounded memory leak
DESCRIPTION: Because sessions are added to the `SESSIONS` dictionary but never removed, the dictionary grows monotonically with every call to `create_session`. In a long-running process, this constitutes an unbounded memory leak that will eventually exhaust available RAM and crash the service.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement session expiration and deletion logic (e.g., via `verify_session` consuming the token or a background cleanup task). In production, use Redis or a similar store with built-in TTL and automatic eviction.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Insecure salt concatenation in password hashing
DESCRIPTION: The `hash_password` function concatenates password and salt directly (`password + salt`) before hashing. While better than no salt, this is not a standard or robust method. Boundary ambiguity between password and salt can cause different credential pairs to produce identical hash inputs.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a standard Key Derivation Function (KDF) like PBKDF2, HMAC-based derivation, or—better yet—switch entirely to a purpose-built password hashing scheme like Argon2 that correctly handles salting and key stretching internally.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: No session invalidation or logout mechanism
DESCRIPTION: There is no function to revoke or delete a session token. Users cannot log out, and compromised tokens cannot be administratively invalidated or revoked, violating the principle of least privilege for session lifecycle management.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add a `revoke_session(token)` function that removes the token from `SESSIONS` and call it on logout or when a security event is detected.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Missing input validation for user_id and password
DESCRIPTION: The `login` and `create_session` functions do not validate that `user_id` or `password` are non-empty strings. Empty strings could create valid sessions mapped to empty user IDs, or an empty password could hash and match if an account has no password set.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add input validation at function entry points to ensure `user_id` and `password` are non-empty strings, raising `ValueError` for invalid inputs.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: design
TITLE: Application domain is hardcoded in callback URL
DESCRIPTION: The `create_session` function hardcodes the domain `https://app.example.com/callback` in the callback URL. This makes the code difficult to configure for different environments (development, staging, production) without modifying the source code itself.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Externalize the domain and callback path into a configuration file or environment variables to make the application flexible across environments.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: urlencode may mishandle complex redirect URLs
DESCRIPTION: While `urlencode` handles standard encoding, complex URLs with fragments or nested query parameters can lead to double-encoding or parsing issues on the receiving end.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `urllib.parse.quote` for the redirect URL value or validate that the redirect URL is a simple path before embedding it in the query string.

---END---

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Use of cryptographically broken MD5 hashing algorithm
DESCRIPTION: The `hash_password` function uses MD5, which is cryptographically broken and computationally fast, making it vulnerable to rainbow table and brute-force attacks. Modern GPUs can compute billions of MD5 hashes per second, making offline attacks trivial if the password database is compromised. This is the most critical security flaw in the module.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace MD5 with a purpose-built password hashing algorithm like bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2id (e.g., via the `argon2-cffi` or `bcrypt` library), which incorporate work factors, built-in salting, and adaptive difficulty.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Password hash comparison vulnerable to timing attacks
DESCRIPTION: The `login` function uses Python's `==` operator to compare the computed hash against the stored hash. The `==` operator performs short-circuiting comparison, exiting early when a byte mismatch is detected. Attackers can measure response time differences to statistically deduce the correct hash byte-by-byte, eventually recovering it and gaining unauthorized access.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `hmac.compare_digest()` or `secrets.compare_digest()` for constant-time comparison of hash strings.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Unvalidated redirect_url parameter enables open redirect attacks
DESCRIPTION: The `redirect_url` parameter is accepted from caller input and embedded directly into the callback URL without validation or allowlisting. An attacker can supply a malicious redirect URL (e.g., `https://evil.com/phish`) to craft legitimate-looking authentication flows that redirect users to attacker-controlled sites, enabling credential phishing.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate the `redirect_url` against a strict allowlist of trusted domains or internal paths before including it in the callback URL.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Session tokens exposed in URL query parameters
DESCRIPTION: The session token is returned as a URL query parameter, causing it to be logged by web servers, proxies, and CDNs; stored in browser history; and leaked via HTTP Referer headers when users navigate to external links. Any of these channels can expose the token to session hijacking.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Transmit session tokens via secure, HTTP-only, SameSite cookies or the Authorization header instead of URL parameters.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: User ID exposed in callback URL
DESCRIPTION: The `uid` parameter is included as a plaintext query parameter in the callback URL. This leaks internal user identifiers to browser history, server logs, and intermediaries. If user IDs are sequential or predictable, this also enables enumeration attacks to probe for valid user IDs.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Remove the `uid` parameter from the callback URL and derive the user identity server-side from the session token using `verify_session()`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: Unbounded session dictionary causes memory exhaustion and allows tokens to persist indefinitely
DESCRIPTION: The `SESSIONS` dictionary grows indefinitely because there is no expiration, TTL, or cleanup logic. This causes two problems: (1) unbounded memory growth that will eventually trigger an Out-Of-Memory kill in production, and (2) stolen or leaked session tokens remain valid forever, giving attackers unlimited access to compromised accounts.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement a TTL (Time-To-Live) mechanism by storing creation timestamps with each session and enforcing a maximum lifetime (e.g., 30 minutes), or use an external store like Redis with automatic key expiration.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: No session invalidation or logout functionality
DESCRIPTION: The module provides no way to delete or revoke a session once created. Users cannot log out to invalidate their sessions, and administrators cannot revoke compromised tokens. This prevents proper session lifecycle management and leaves the system vulnerable to prolonged access with stolen tokens.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement a `revoke_session(token)` function that removes the session entry from the store, enabling logout and token revocation on security events.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: In-memory session store is unsafe under concurrent access and multi-process deployment
DESCRIPTION: The in-memory dictionary works only within a single process. In typical production deployments with multiple web worker processes (e.g., gunicorn with multiple workers) or async frameworks with concurrent coroutines, a session created in one process will be invisible to others, causing intermittent authentication failures. Additionally, in multi-threaded environments, concurrent read-modify-write operations on the dict lack synchronization, creating race conditions.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace the in-memory dictionary with a centralized, atomic data store like Redis or a database. Alternatively, add explicit thread-safe locking around all dictionary operations.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: No brute-force or rate-limit protection on login attempts
DESCRIPTION: The `login` function accepts an unbounded number of authentication attempts with no throttling, lockout, or delay. An attacker can rapidly guess passwords without consequence. Combined with the broken MD5 hashing, this makes online brute-force attacks practical.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement rate limiting (e.g., per-IP or per-user-ID) and account lockout after a configurable number of failed authentication attempts within a time window.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Salt parameter is not validated for randomness or strength
DESCRIPTION: The `hash_password` function accepts a `salt` parameter without validating its format, length, randomness, or entropy. This allows callers to pass weak, predictable, or reused salts across multiple users, enabling precomputation attacks and reducing the protection that salting provides.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Generate a cryptographically secure random salt (e.g., 16+ bytes) internally for each password during registration, store the salt alongside the hash, and pass only the stored salt during verification.

SEVERITY: low

findings.title: Use of cryptographically broken MD5 hashing algorithm
findings.description: The `hash_password` function uses MD5, which is cryptographically broken and computationally fast, making it vulnerable to rainbow table and brute-force attacks. Modern GPUs can compute billions of MD5 hashes per second, making offline attacks trivial if the password database is compromised. This is the most critical security flaw in the module.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace MD5 with a purpose-built password hashing algorithm like bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2id (e.g., via the `argon2-cffi` or `bcrypt` library), which incorporate work factors, built-in salting, and adaptive difficulty.

findings.title: Password hash comparison vulnerable to timing attacks
findings.description: The `login` function uses Python's `==` operator to compare the computed hash against the stored hash. The `==` operator performs short-circuiting comparison, exiting early when a byte mismatch is detected. Attackers can measure response time differences to statistically deduce the correct hash byte-by-byte, eventually recovering it and gaining unauthorized access.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `hmac.compare_digest()` or `secrets.compare_digest()` for constant-time comparison of hash strings.

findings.title: Unbounded session dictionary causes memory exhaustion and allows tokens to persist indefinitely
findings.description: The `SESSIONS` dictionary grows indefinitely because there is no expiration, TTL, or cleanup logic. This causes two problems: (1) unbounded memory growth that will eventually trigger an Out-Of-Memory kill in production, and (2) stolen or leaked session tokens remain valid forever, giving attackers unlimited access to compromised accounts.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement a TTL (Time-To-Live) mechanism by storing creation timestamps with each session and enforcing a maximum lifetime (e.g., 30 minutes), or use an external store like Redis with automatic key expiration.

findings.title: In-memory session store is unsafe under concurrent access and multi-process deployment
findings.description: The in-memory dictionary works only within a single process. In typical production deployments with multiple web worker processes (e.g., gunicorn with multiple workers) or async frameworks with concurrent coroutines, a session created in one process will be invisible to others, causing intermittent authentication failures. Additionally, in multi-threaded environments, concurrent read-modify-write operations on the dict lack synchronization, creating race conditions.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the in-memory dictionary with a centralized, atomic data store like Redis or a database. Alternatively, add explicit thread-safe locking around all dictionary operations.

SUGGESTED_FIX: Deliver the session token via a `Set-Cookie` header with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite=Strict` attributes instead of embedding it in the URL.
