DESCRIPTION: `login` compares `hash_password(password, salt) == stored_hash` with Python's built-in `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. This creates a timing oracle that allows an attacker to infer character-by-character matches through statistical measurement of response times.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `hmac.compare_digest(hash_password(password, salt), stored_hash)` for constant-time comparison.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Salt concatenated before password — trivially bypassed prepend attack
DESCRIPTION: `hash_password` computes `MD5(password + salt)`, meaning the salt is appended after the password. A fixed-prefix attack can partially precompute rainbow tables. The canonical form is `hash(salt + password)`, but more importantly, using a proper KDF makes this moot — the KDF controls salt integration internally.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Switch to a proper KDF (argon2, bcrypt, scrypt) which handles salt incorporation correctly and securely.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Sessions never expire — no TTL or invalidation mechanism
DESCRIPTION: `SESSIONS` stores tokens indefinitely. A stolen token remains valid forever. There is no logout, no expiry, and no way to revoke a compromised session. This violates the principle of least privilege for session lifetime.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Store sessions with an expiry timestamp and reject tokens past their TTL; for the Redis production path, use `SETEX` with an appropriate TTL (e.g., 15–60 minutes).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Unsynchronized read-write on shared `SESSIONS` dict
DESCRIPTION: `SESSIONS` is a module-level mutable dict accessed by `create_session` (write) and `verify_session` (read) from potentially multiple threads. In CPython the GIL protects individual bytecode operations but not compound read-modify-write sequences, and alternative runtimes (PyPy, no-GIL CPython 3.13+) offer no such protection. Under concurrent load, this is a data race.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Protect `SESSIONS` with a `threading.Lock`, or — since the comment notes Redis for production — ensure all access goes through Redis atomically.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Token entropy is only 128 bits — acceptable but no uniqueness check
DESCRIPTION: `secrets.token_hex(16)` produces 128 bits of entropy. While statistically unlikely, there is no collision check before inserting into `SESSIONS`. A collision silently overwrites the existing user's session, effectively logging them out and potentially handing the token to a new user.
SUGGESTED_FIX: After generating the token, check `if token not in SESSIONS` before storing; retry generation on the rare collision, or increase to `token_hex(32)` for 256-bit tokens.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: Session not rotated after successful authentication
DESCRIPTION: `login` calls `create_session` which generates a new token, but if a pre-authentication session token existed (e.g., from an anonymous session), it is not invalidated. More broadly, the pattern does not prevent session fixation: an attacker who can set a victim's token before login retains access after login.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Invalidate any prior session associated with the user before issuing a new token; ensure the new token is generated only after credentials are verified (already the case here, but fixation via other paths must be blocked).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: `redirect_url` scheme not validated — javascript: URI possible
DESCRIPTION: Beyond open redirect, `redirect_url` could be `javascript:alert(1)` or `data:text/html,...`. If the returned URL is rendered as an `<a href>` or used in a `window.location` assignment by the frontend, this enables XSS.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Enforce that `redirect_url` starts with `https://` and matches an allowlisted host before including it.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: `user_id` accepted as plain string with no validation
DESCRIPTION: `create_session` and `login` accept arbitrary `user_id` strings. There is no length cap, character validation, or sanitisation. A caller passing a very large string, a null byte, or injection payload will have it stored in `SESSIONS` and embedded in the URL.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate `user_id` format (e.g., UUID, alphanumeric, max 128 chars) at the boundary before processing.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: In-memory `SESSIONS` grows without bound — memory exhaustion
DESCRIPTION: Every call to `create_session` adds an entry that is never removed. Under normal usage with expiring sessions this eventually grows unboundedly. Under an unauthenticated flood (attacker calling the endpoint repeatedly), this is a trivial memory exhaustion DoS vector.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Enforce a maximum session count or, better, implement TTL-based eviction; rate-limit session creation per IP/user.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `login` creates session before confirming `user_id` existence
DESCRIPTION: `login` assumes `user_id` is valid and authoritative — it only checks the password hash. There is no lookup of the actual user record; a caller could pass any `user_id` string paired with a matching `stored_hash` and fabricate a session for a non-existent or different account.
SUGGESTED_FIX: The caller should retrieve the user record (including `stored_hash` and `salt`) by `user_id` from the data store before calling `login`, so the function verifies a record that was actually fetched for that identity.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: No logging on authentication failure or success
DESCRIPTION: Failed login attempts, successful authentications, and session creations produce no log output. This makes it impossible to detect brute-force attacks, audit access, or investigate incidents after the fact.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Log authentication outcomes (success/failure, user ID, source IP) at appropriate log levels, being careful never to log the password or token.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Empty or whitespace `password` and `salt` accepted silently
DESCRIPTION: `hash_password` does not reject empty strings. An empty password hashes to a fixed value, and an empty salt provides no randomness. A misconfigured caller passing `salt=""` or `password=""` will produce a deterministic hash with zero protection.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Raise `ValueError` if `password` or `salt` is empty; enforce a minimum salt length (≥16 bytes of random data).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: security
TITLE: `salt` should be generated internally, not passed by caller
DESCRIPTION: The API surface for `hash_password` and `login` requires the caller to supply the salt. This delegates a security-critical responsibility to callers who may pass weak, reused, or empty salts. Password hashing libraries (bcrypt, argon2) generate and embed the salt automatically.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a KDF that manages the salt internally and returns an opaque hash string (e.g., `argon2.PasswordHasher().hash(password)`).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: design
TITLE: `SESSIONS` dict is module-level global — untestable and stateful
DESCRIPTION: Module-level mutable state makes unit testing difficult (tests bleed into each other), prevents horizontal scaling (state is per-process), and violates dependency injection principles. The comment acknowledges this but the design choice permeates the API.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Accept a session store object (implementing a simple `get`/`set`/`delete` interface) as a parameter or dependency, defaulting to a local dict only in tests.

---END---

findings.title: MD5 used for password hashing — cryptographically broken
findings.description: `hash_password` uses MD5, which is not a password hashing function. MD5 is extremely fast, making brute-force and rainbow-table attacks trivial. It has also been cryptographically broken (collision attacks) for decades. Password storage requires a deliberately slow, memory-hard KDF.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with `bcrypt`, `argon2-cffi`, or `hashlib.scrypt`/`hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac` with a high iteration count; never use MD5 or SHA-family hashes for passwords.

findings.title: Session token exposed in redirect URL query string
findings.description: `create_session` appends the bearer token as a plain query-string parameter (`?session=<token>`). Query strings appear in browser history, server access logs, referrer headers, and proxy logs. Any intermediary or user with access to logs can steal the session token and hijack the account.
findings.suggested_fix: Deliver the session token via a `Set-Cookie` header with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite=Strict` attributes instead of embedding it in the URL.

findings.title: `user_id` leaked in unauthenticated redirect URL
findings.description: The `uid` parameter passes the raw `user_id` in the redirect URL before the session is validated by the receiving endpoint. This exposes PII/account identifiers in logs, history, and referrer chains unnecessarily. The receiver already has the token and can look up the user itself.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove `uid` from the URL parameters entirely; the receiving endpoint should resolve the user via `verify_session(token)`.

findings.title: Open redirect — attacker-controlled `redirect_url` embedded in response
findings.description: `redirect_url` comes from the caller (ultimately user input) and is placed directly into the returned URL without any validation. An attacker can pass `redirect_url=https://evil.com` to craft a URL that sends victims to a malicious site after authentication, enabling phishing and credential harvesting.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate `redirect_url` against an allowlist of trusted origins before including it; reject or strip any URL whose scheme+host is not explicitly permitted.

raw:
---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Unsynchronized list append from multiple threads
DESCRIPTION: `self._results` is a plain `list` appended to concurrently by every worker thread in `_worker_loop`. CPython's GIL makes individual `list.append` calls atomic today, but this is an implementation detail, not a language guarantee. On other runtimes (PyPy STM, GraalPy, the nogil/free-threaded CPython 3.13+) concurrent appends can corrupt the list or lose items. Even on current CPython, relying on GIL atomicity is a well-known anti-pattern that breaks silently when the runtime changes.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Protect `self._results` with a `threading.Lock`, or replace it with a `queue.Queue` dedicated to results.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `_stop` flag read without memory barrier or lock
DESCRIPTION: `self._stop` is a plain `bool` written by the main thread in `shutdown()` and read by every worker thread in `_worker_loop`. There is no lock, `threading.Event`, or other synchronization primitive ensuring visibility across threads. On free-threaded CPython (PEP 703) or non-CPython runtimes, a worker may never observe the updated value due to CPU-level caching/reordering, causing `shutdown()` to hang forever on `join()`.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace `self._stop` with a `threading.Event` and use `event.is_set()` / `event.set()`, which provides proper cross-thread visibility.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Shutdown discards jobs still queued but not yet processed
DESCRIPTION: `shutdown()` sets the stop flag immediately and joins workers. Workers exit their loop as soon as `_stop` is `True`, even if items remain in the queue. Any submitted-but-unprocessed jobs are silently dropped, with no indication to the caller that work was lost.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Drain the queue before stopping, or use a sentinel/poison-pill approach: put `None` into the queue for each worker and have workers exit when they dequeue `None`, guaranteeing all prior items are processed.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `get_results` returns mutable internal list without copying
DESCRIPTION: `get_results()` returns a direct reference to `self._results`. The caller can mutate it (clear, pop, insert) while workers are still appending, leading to unpredictable behavior. Even read-only iteration by the caller can raise `RuntimeError` if the list changes size during iteration on some runtimes.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Return a shallow copy (`return list(self._results)`) and acquire the results lock while copying.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: No way to wait for a specific job's result
DESCRIPTION: Results are appended into a flat list keyed only by `fn.__name__`. If the same function is submitted multiple times, there is no way to correlate which result belongs to which submission. There is also no mechanism (e.g., `Future`, `Event`) to block until a particular job completes, making the pool unsuitable for most real workloads.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Return a `Future`-like object from `submit()` that the caller can `await`/`.result()` on, or at minimum include a unique job ID in each result tuple.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: `fn.__name__` may not exist or may be unhelpful
DESCRIPTION: The code accesses `fn.__name__` to tag results. Lambdas all share the name `<lambda>`, `functools.partial` objects have no `__name__` (raises `AttributeError`), and arbitrary callables (classes with `__call__`) may also lack it. This causes an unhandled `AttributeError` that is itself caught by the broad `except Exception`, masking the real result and producing a misleading error entry.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `getattr(fn, '__name__', repr(fn))` to safely obtain an identifier, or store the callable reference itself.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `num_workers` accepts zero or negative values
DESCRIPTION: If `num_workers=0` is passed, no threads are created and all submitted jobs silently accumulate in the queue forever, never executing. Negative values are similarly accepted without error. This is a silent misconfiguration that is hard to debug.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate `num_workers >= 1` in `__init__` and raise `ValueError` otherwise.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Pool can be used after shutdown
DESCRIPTION: After `shutdown()` is called, `submit()` still happily enqueues new jobs into `self._queue`. These jobs will never be processed because all worker threads have exited. There is no guard or error to prevent post-shutdown submission.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Set a `_shutdown` flag and raise `RuntimeError` in `submit()` if the pool has been shut down.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: Exceptions are stringified, losing traceback and type
DESCRIPTION: In the `except Exception as e` block, the exception is coerced to `f"ERROR: {e}"`. This discards the exception type, traceback, and chained exceptions. Callers cannot distinguish between a job that returned the string `"ERROR: ..."` and one that actually failed, nor can they re-raise or inspect the original exception.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Store the actual exception object (or `sys.exc_info()`) in the results tuple, and use a distinct field or wrapper to differentiate success from failure.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `queue.get` result never acknowledged with `task_done`
DESCRIPTION: The code calls `self._queue.get()` but never calls `self._queue.task_done()`. If any caller ever uses `self._queue.join()` (a natural extension for waiting on completion), it will block forever because the internal unfinished-task counter is never decremented.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Call `self._queue.task_done()` in a `finally` block after processing each item.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: No context-manager protocol for automatic cleanup
DESCRIPTION: The pool creates daemon threads but provides no `__enter__`/`__exit__` methods. If a caller forgets to call `shutdown()`, worker threads persist as daemon threads until process exit, potentially leaving jobs half-finished or resources unclosed. The pattern is error-prone compared to a context manager.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement `__enter__` returning `self` and `__exit__` calling `self.shutdown()` so the pool can be used with `with WorkerPool() as pool:`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Double shutdown causes harmless but wasteful re-join
DESCRIPTION: Calling `shutdown()` twice will attempt to `join()` already-dead threads. While this doesn't raise an error, it is wasteful and indicates missing idempotency tracking that could mask bugs in more complex lifecycle management.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Guard `shutdown()` with a flag that short-circuits on repeated calls.

---END---

findings.title: Unsynchronized list append from multiple threads
findings.description: `self._results` is a plain `list` appended to concurrently by every worker thread in `_worker_loop`. CPython's GIL makes individual `list.append` calls atomic today, but this is an implementation detail, not a language guarantee. On other runtimes (PyPy STM, GraalPy, the nogil/free-threaded CPython 3.13+) concurrent appends can corrupt the list or lose items. Even on current CPython, relying on GIL atomicity is a well-known anti-pattern that breaks silently when the runtime changes.
findings.suggested_fix: Protect `self._results` with a `threading.Lock`, or replace it with a `queue.Queue` dedicated to results.

findings.title: Shutdown discards jobs still queued but not yet processed
findings.description: `shutdown()` sets the stop flag immediately and joins workers. Workers exit their loop as soon as `_stop` is `True`, even if items remain in the queue. Any submitted-but-unprocessed jobs are silently dropped, with no indication to the caller that work was lost.
findings.suggested_fix: Drain the queue before stopping, or use a sentinel/poison-pill approach: put `None` into the queue for each worker and have workers exit when they dequeue `None`, guaranteeing all prior items are processed.

raw:
# Deduplicated Code Review Findings

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Unsynchronized concurrent access to `_results` list causes data races
DESCRIPTION: Multiple worker threads call `self._results.append(...)` without synchronization. While CPython's GIL makes a single append atomic, `get_results()` returns a live reference to the internal list. Callers iterating over it while workers append concurrently can observe partially-updated lists, raise `RuntimeError: list changed size during iteration`, or corrupt data. Callers can also directly modify the returned list, causing further race conditions.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Protect all accesses to `_results` with a `threading.Lock`. Have `get_results()` return a shallow copy `return list(self._results)` taken under that lock.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Non-thread-safe `_stop` flag causes visibility and race condition issues
DESCRIPTION: The `_stop` boolean is read and written across threads without synchronization. While CPython's GIL makes assignment atomic, there is no memory-visibility guarantee that workers will see the updated value promptly, especially on other Python implementations. This delays or prevents shutdown signal delivery.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace `_stop` with a `threading.Event` (`_stop_event`); workers check `_stop_event.is_set()` and `shutdown()` calls `_stop_event.set()`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: Unbounded `_results` list causes indefinite memory growth
DESCRIPTION: The `_results` list appends every job result with no cleanup or size limit. In long-running pools, memory consumption grows unboundedly until the process crashes or starves the system.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Provide a `clear_results()` method, use a bounded `collections.deque(maxlen=N)`, or document a consume-and-clear contract for callers.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: Unbounded job queue defaults to infinite size
DESCRIPTION: `queue.Queue()` defaults to unbounded size. If jobs are submitted faster than workers process them, memory usage grows indefinitely until the process crashes.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Initialize the queue with a reasonable `maxsize` parameter to apply backpressure and prevent runaway growth.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `shutdown()` leaves queued jobs silently unprocessed
DESCRIPTION: Setting `_stop = True` causes workers to exit at the next timeout boundary (up to 1 second later). Any jobs still queued are never executed and no error is raised. Callers have no visibility into abandoned work.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Before setting the stop flag, drain remaining queue items via `_queue.join()` (requires `task_done()` calls), or add a `wait=True` parameter that synchronizes completion.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Workers never call `queue.task_done()`, breaking join semantics
DESCRIPTION: `queue.Queue.join()` blocks until every put item has a corresponding `task_done()` call. Since `_worker_loop` never calls `task_done()`, any use of `_queue.join()` to wait for completion will deadlock indefinitely. This prevents clean drain-before-stop patterns.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add `self._queue.task_done()` in a `finally` block inside `_worker_loop`, after the job is processed (success or failure).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Multiple `shutdown()` calls cause `RuntimeError` on re-join
DESCRIPTION: Calling `shutdown()` twice attempts to join already-joined threads, raising a `RuntimeError`. This breaks idempotent cleanup and crashes graceful shutdown sequences.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add a `_shutdown_flag` and use `threading.Lock` to guard `shutdown()`, making it idempotent and thread-safe.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: `shutdown()` deadlocks indefinitely with long-running or blocked jobs
DESCRIPTION: `w.join()` blocks indefinitely with no timeout. If a submitted job never returns (infinite loop, blocking I/O, internal deadlock), `shutdown()` hangs forever. No mechanism exists to interrupt or kill worker threads.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Pass a `timeout` parameter to `w.join()` and document that submitted callables must be finite, or expose a cancel/interrupt mechanism.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `submit()` allows enqueuing jobs after `shutdown()` is called
DESCRIPTION: Jobs can be enqueued after `shutdown()` has been called. Since workers have already exited, these jobs are lost silently or processed by lingering threads. No exception is raised and the caller may believe work was accepted.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Check the shutdown flag in `submit()` and raise `RuntimeError("pool is shut down")` if the pool is no longer active.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: `fn.__name__` raises `AttributeError` for lambdas and `functools.partial`
DESCRIPTION: Lambda objects have `__name__ == '<lambda>'` (acceptable but ambiguous), while `functools.partial` objects lack `__name__` entirely, causing an `AttributeError` that crashes the worker thread. This halts processing for that job and makes debugging difficult.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `getattr(fn, '__name__', repr(fn))` to safely retrieve the function name without raising exceptions.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Zero or negative `num_workers` creates a broken pool silently
DESCRIPTION: Passing `num_workers <= 0` results in an empty worker list. Submitted jobs are queued forever and never executed. `shutdown()` returns immediately. No `ValueError` is raised and the caller may assume work is being done.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add validation in `__init__`: `if num_workers < 1: raise ValueError(f"num_workers must be >= 1, got {num_workers}")`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Error results are indistinguishable from legitimate string return values
DESCRIPTION: When a job raises an exception, the result is stored as a plain string `"ERROR: <msg>"`. If a job legitimately returns a string beginning with `"ERROR: "`, the caller cannot tell success from failure, making the API unreliable.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Store results as typed objects, e.g., a `JobResult(status, value)` dataclass with explicit `"ok"` / `"error"` status, or use a custom `JobError` sentinel class.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: Exceptions in jobs are silently swallowed with no logging
DESCRIPTION: Worker exceptions are caught and stored as strings but never logged. If no one calls `get_results()` and inspects every entry, failures are invisible. In long-running pools this makes debugging extremely difficult.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add `logging.exception(...)` or `logging.error(...)` inside the except block so failures surface in application logs immediately.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: performance
TITLE: Polling loop with timeout wastes CPU and delays shutdown
DESCRIPTION: Workers rely on `queue.get(timeout=1.0)` and spin on `queue.Empty`. This delays shutdown by up to 1 second per worker and wastes CPU cycles during idle periods.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `threading.Event` to signal workers to wake up immediately, or use `queue.join()` with sentinel values for clean termination.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Daemon flag contradicts explicit `shutdown()` contract
DESCRIPTION: Threads are marked as `daemon=True`, causing them to terminate abruptly when the main thread exits. This contradicts the explicit `shutdown()` join contract and can cause silent data loss or incomplete processing.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Remove `daemon=True` if `shutdown()` is intended to be called, or document that `shutdown()` is optional and daemons will be killed on exit.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: design
TITLE: No way to retrieve result for a specific submitted job
DESCRIPTION: All results are aggregated in a single list keyed only by function name. Callers cannot correlate a result to a specific `submit()` call. Multiple calls to the same function produce duplicate ambiguous keys, making the API unsuitable for anything beyond fire-and-forget homogeneous jobs.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Return a `Future`-like object from `submit()` that the caller can `.result()` on, or assign a unique job ID and expose `get_result(job_id)`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: design
TITLE: No context manager support (`__enter__` / `__exit__`)
DESCRIPTION: The pool manages threads but is not usable as a context manager, making it easy to forget `shutdown()` calls in exception paths, leading to thread leaks and resource exhaustion.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement `__enter__` returning `self` and `__exit__` calling `self.shutdown()` to guarantee cleanup.

---END---

findings.suggested_fix: Before setting the stop flag, drain remaining queue items via `_queue.join()` (requires `task_done()` calls), or add a `wait=True` parameter that synchronizes completion.
findings.raw_block:
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `shutdown()` leaves queued jobs silently unprocessed
DESCRIPTION: Setting `_stop = True` causes workers to exit at the next timeout boundary (up to 1 second later). Any jobs still queued are never executed and no error is raised. Callers have no visibility into abandoned work.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Before setting the stop flag, drain remaining queue items via `_queue.join()` (requires `task_done()` calls), or add a `wait=True` parameter that synchronizes completion.

findings.title: Workers never call `queue.task_done()`, breaking join semantics
findings.description: `queue.Queue.join()` blocks until every put item has a corresponding `task_done()` call. Since `_worker_loop` never calls `task_done()`, any use of `_queue.join()` to wait for completion will deadlock indefinitely. This prevents clean drain-before-stop patterns.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `self._queue.task_done()` in a `finally` block inside `_worker_loop`, after the job is processed (success or failure).

SUGGESTED_FIX: Add `self._queue.task_done()` in a `finally` block inside `_worker_loop`, after the job is processed (success or failure).

findings.title: Multiple `shutdown()` calls cause `RuntimeError` on re-join
findings.description: Calling `shutdown()` twice attempts to join already-joined threads, raising a `RuntimeError`. This breaks idempotent cleanup and crashes graceful shutdown sequences.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a `_shutdown_flag` and use `threading.Lock` to guard `shutdown()`, making it idempotent and thread-safe.

SUGGESTED_FIX: Add a `_shutdown_flag` and use `threading.Lock` to guard `shutdown()`, making it idempotent and thread-safe.

findings.title: `shutdown()` deadlocks indefinitely with long-running or blocked jobs
findings.description: `w.join()` blocks indefinitely with no timeout. If a submitted job never returns (infinite loop, blocking I/O, internal deadlock), `shutdown()` hangs forever. No mechanism exists to interrupt or kill worker threads.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass a `timeout` parameter to `w.join()` and document that submitted callables must be finite, or expose a cancel/interrupt mechanism.

SUGGESTED_FIX: Pass a `timeout` parameter to `w.join()` and document that submitted callables must be finite, or expose a cancel/interrupt mechanism.

findings.title: `submit()` allows enqueuing jobs after `shutdown()` is called
findings.description: Jobs can be enqueued after `shutdown()` has been called. Since workers have already exited, these jobs are lost silently or processed by lingering threads. No exception is raised and the caller may believe work was accepted.
findings.suggested_fix: Check the shutdown flag in `submit()` and raise `RuntimeError("pool is shut down")` if the pool is no longer active.

findings.title: `fn.__name__` raises `AttributeError` for lambdas and `functools.partial`
findings.description: Lambda objects have `__name__ == '<lambda>'` (acceptable but ambiguous), while `functools.partial` objects lack `__name__` entirely, causing an `AttributeError` that crashes the worker thread. This halts processing for that job and makes debugging difficult.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `getattr(fn, '__name__', repr(fn))` to safely retrieve the function name without raising exceptions.

findings.title: Zero or negative `num_workers` creates a broken pool silently
findings.description: Passing `num_workers <= 0` results in an empty worker list. Submitted jobs are queued forever and never executed. `shutdown()` returns immediately. No `ValueError` is raised and the caller may assume work is being done.
findings.suggested_fix: Add validation in `__init__`: `if num_workers < 1: raise ValueError(f"num_workers must be >= 1, got {num_workers}")`.

findings.title: Error results are indistinguishable from legitimate string return values
findings.description: When a job raises an exception, the result is stored as a plain string `"ERROR: <msg>"`. If a job legitimately returns a string beginning with `"ERROR: "`, the caller cannot tell success from failure, making the API unreliable.
findings.suggested_fix: Store results as typed objects, e.g., a `JobResult(status, value)` dataclass with explicit `"ok"` / `"error"` status, or use a custom `JobError` sentinel class.

findings.title: Exceptions in jobs are silently swallowed with no logging
findings.description: Worker exceptions are caught and stored as strings but never logged. If no one calls `get_results()` and inspects every entry, failures are invisible. In long-running pools this makes debugging extremely difficult.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `logging.exception(...)` or `logging.error(...)` inside the except block so failures surface in application logs immediately.

findings.title: Polling loop with timeout wastes CPU and delays shutdown
findings.description: Workers rely on `queue.get(timeout=1.0)` and spin on `queue.Empty`. This delays shutdown by up to 1 second per worker and wastes CPU cycles during idle periods.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `threading.Event` to signal workers to wake up immediately, or use `queue.join()` with sentinel values for clean termination.

findings.title: Daemon flag contradicts explicit `shutdown()` contract
findings.description: Threads are marked as `daemon=True`, causing them to terminate abruptly when the main thread exits. This contradicts the explicit `shutdown()` join contract and can cause silent data loss or incomplete processing.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove `daemon=True` if `shutdown()` is intended to be called, or document that `shutdown()` is optional and daemons will be killed on exit.

findings.title: No way to retrieve result for a specific submitted job
findings.description: All results are aggregated in a single list keyed only by function name. Callers cannot correlate a result to a specific `submit()` call. Multiple calls to the same function produce duplicate ambiguous keys, making the API unsuitable for anything beyond fire-and-forget homogeneous jobs.
findings.suggested_fix: Return a `Future`-like object from `submit()` that the caller can `.result()` on, or assign a unique job ID and expose `get_result(job_id)`.

findings.title: No context manager support (`__enter__` / `__exit__`)
findings.description: The pool manages threads but is not usable as a context manager, making it easy to forget `shutdown()` calls in exception paths, leading to thread leaks and resource exhaustion.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement `__enter__` returning `self` and `__exit__` calling `self.shutdown()` to guarantee cleanup.

raw:
Poniżej znajduje się skonsolidowana lista deduplikowanych wniosków z trzech niezależnych recenzji:

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Unsynchronized writes to shared results list cause race condition.
DESCRIPTION: Multiple worker threads append to `self._results` without synchronization. While CPython's GIL makes `list.append` atomic today, this is an implementation detail not guaranteed by the language. On free-threaded CPython (3.13+ nogil), PyPy with STM, GraalPy, or alternative runtimes, concurrent appends can corrupt the list, lose entries, or raise RuntimeError. Relying on the GIL for thread-safety is a well-known anti-pattern that silently breaks when the runtime changes. Additionally, `get_results()` returns a direct reference to this list, allowing callers to iterate while workers append concurrently, causing further data races.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Protect all accesses to `self._results` with a `threading.Lock`, or switch to a `queue.Queue` for results. Ensure `get_results()` returns a copy under the lock: `with self._lock: return list(self._results)`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: Unbounded job queue causes uncontrolled memory growth.
DESCRIPTION: The job queue is initialized without a maxsize parameter, allowing unlimited queueing. If jobs are submitted faster than workers can process them, memory usage spikes and can exhaust available RAM, causing application crashes or OOM kills in containerized environments.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Initialize the queue with a reasonable maxsize parameter (e.g., `maxsize=1000`) or implement backpressure logic to block or reject submissions when the queue is full.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Shutdown process does not drain queued jobs, causing silent data loss.
DESCRIPTION: The `shutdown()` method signals workers to stop by setting `_stop = True` and joining threads, but workers exit their loop immediately upon seeing the stop flag, even if items remain in the queue. Jobs that have been submitted but not yet dequeued are silently discarded with no notification to the caller, leading to unexpected data loss.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a sentinel/poison-pill pattern (inject `None` into the queue for each worker) or implement graceful queue draining with `queue.task_done()` / `queue.join()` to ensure all submitted work completes before shutdown returns.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Stop flag read without memory barrier causes unreliable shutdown.
DESCRIPTION: `self._stop` is a plain `bool` written by the main thread and read by workers without synchronization. Python does not guarantee visibility of writes across threads for plain attributes. On free-threaded CPython (3.13+ nogil) or non-CPython runtimes, workers may never observe the updated value due to CPU-level caching. Even under the GIL, the pattern is fragile and unsafe for production.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace `self._stop` with a `threading.Event` (e.g., `self._stop_event = threading.Event()` and check `self._stop_event.is_set()` in the worker loop).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Shutdown delayed by queue timeout polling instead of using sentinels.
DESCRIPTION: Workers block on `queue.get(timeout=1.0)`, checking the `_stop` flag only after the timeout expires when the queue is empty. This causes shutdown to be delayed by up to one second per worker, making graceful termination slow. Calling `shutdown()` multiple times also introduces issues as workers may already be terminated.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a sentinel/poison-pill pattern: append `None` to the queue for each worker so they unblock immediately. Guard `shutdown()` with a state flag to ensure idempotency.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `get_results()` returns mutable internal list allowing unsafe concurrent access.
DESCRIPTION: The method returns a direct reference to `self._results`. Callers can iterate over this list while worker threads append to it concurrently, causing `RuntimeError` (list changed size during iteration), data races, or inconsistent views. Callers can also modify or clear the list, corrupting internal state and losing results.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Return a shallow copy under a lock: `with self._lock: return list(self._results)`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `submit()` allows adding jobs after `shutdown()` has been called.
DESCRIPTION: There is no mechanism to prevent job submission after shutdown. Jobs submitted after `shutdown()` will queue but never process, as workers are terminating. Calling `shutdown()` multiple times also leaves the pool in an inconsistent state with no clear feedback.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add a state flag (e.g., `self._shutting_down`) set in `shutdown()`. Have `submit()` check this flag and raise `RuntimeError` if the pool is closed. Guard shutdown with a lock for idempotency.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Function names used as result keys cause collisions and ambiguity.
DESCRIPTION: Results are keyed by `fn.__name__`, which is not unique across different functions. Multiple jobs using the same function will overwrite previous results. Lambdas all share the name `<lambda>`, making it impossible to distinguish results from different lambda invocations.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Assign a unique job ID in `submit()` and return it. Store results in a dictionary keyed by job ID.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Pool cannot be used as a context manager for proper resource cleanup.
DESCRIPTION: There is no `__enter__` / `__exit__` implementation. If an exception occurs between pool creation and `shutdown()`, daemon threads are left running indefinitely and submitted work is silently lost. This violates Python conventions for resource-managing objects.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement `__enter__` and `__exit__` methods to support the `with WorkerPool() as pool:` idiom, calling `shutdown()` in `__exit__`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: No mechanism to track when submitted work is complete.
DESCRIPTION: There is no way for callers to wait for a specific job's completion or know when all pending work has finished. The underlying `queue.Queue` supports `task_done()` / `join()` semantics, but neither is called. This makes the pool unsuitable for use cases requiring asynchronous work tracking.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Call `self._queue.task_done()` after each job completes and expose a `wait()` method that calls `self._queue.join()`. Alternatively, return `concurrent.futures.Future` objects from `submit()`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: Exception handling loses traceback and context, hindering debugging.
DESCRIPTION: When a worker catches an exception, it stores only a formatted string (e.g., `f"ERROR: {e}"`) in results, discarding exception type, traceback, and stack frames. This critical debugging information is lost, making root cause diagnosis extremely difficult in production. Additionally, this string is indistinguishable from a job that legitimately returns a string starting with "ERROR:".
SUGGESTED_FIX: Store the full exception object and traceback (e.g., `{'status': 'error', 'exception': e, 'traceback': traceback.format_exc()}`). Add `logging.exception()` calls and consider returning `Future` objects to distinguish success from failure.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: Constructor does not validate `num_workers` parameter.
DESCRIPTION: The `__init__` method accepts zero or negative values for `num_workers` without validation. If `num_workers <= 0`, the pool creates no worker threads and becomes non-functional. Submitted jobs queue indefinitely and never execute, causing silent hangs with no error alerting the developer.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add a check in `__init__` to validate that `num_workers >= 1` and raise `ValueError` if the constraint is violated.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: Results list grows indefinitely, risking unbounded memory consumption.
DESCRIPTION: The `_results` list accumulates results for the entire lifetime of the `WorkerPool` instance without any size limit or expiration policy. For long-running services or tasks producing large results, this leads to unbounded memory growth separate from the queue buffering issue.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement a mechanism to cap the size of `_results` (e.g., using `collections.deque` with maxlen) or provide a method for users to clear results periodically (e.g., `clear_results()`).

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Daemon threads cause silent job loss on main thread exit.
DESCRIPTION: Workers are created with `daemon=True`, meaning they are abruptly killed when the main thread exits. Any pending or in-flight jobs are discarded without warning or cleanup, potentially leading to partially processed data or resource leaks.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Remove `daemon=True` or implement a proper context manager to ensure graceful shutdown before program termination.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: `fn.__name__` attribute access fails for some callable types.
DESCRIPTION: The code uses `fn.__name__` to tag results, but some callable types lack this attribute. `functools.partial` objects raise `AttributeError`, and callable classes may not define `__name__`. When this fails, the exception is caught by the broad `except Exception`, masking the real error.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `getattr(fn, '__name__', repr(fn))` to safely obtain a label for any callable, falling back to `repr(fn)` when `__name__` is unavailable.

---END---

DESCRIPTION: There is no mechanism to prevent job submission after shutdown. Jobs submitted after `shutdown()` will queue but never process, as workers are terminating. Calling `shutdown()` multiple times also leaves the pool in an inconsistent state with no clear feedback.

findings.description: Results are keyed by `fn.__name__`, which is not unique across different functions. Multiple jobs using the same function will overwrite previous results. Lambdas all share the name `<lambda>`, making it impossible to distinguish results from different lambda invocations.
findings.suggested_fix: Assign a unique job ID in `submit()` and return it. Store results in a dictionary keyed by job ID.

findings.title: Pool cannot be used as a context manager for proper resource cleanup.
findings.description: There is no `__enter__` / `__exit__` implementation. If an exception occurs between pool creation and `shutdown()`, daemon threads are left running indefinitely and submitted work is silently lost. This violates Python conventions for resource-managing objects.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement `__enter__` and `__exit__` methods to support the `with WorkerPool() as pool:` idiom, calling `shutdown()` in `__exit__`.

findings.title: Exception handling loses traceback and context, hindering debugging.

raw:
Looking at all three reviewer reports, I'll identify and merge the duplicate findings, keeping unique ones, and synthesize a comprehensive list.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Thread-unsafe access to _results list causes data corruption and RuntimeErrors
DESCRIPTION: The `_results` list is appended to concurrently by every worker thread without synchronization. While CPython's GIL makes `list.append` atomically safe at the bytecode level, this is not a language guarantee and fails on PyPy with STM, GraalPy, and free-threaded CPython 3.13+. Even on standard CPython, callers iterating over the list returned by `get_results` while workers append will trigger `RuntimeError: list changed size during iteration`. This is both a concurrency bug and an encapsulation violation.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Protect `_results` with a `threading.Lock`, return a shallow copy in `get_results()` (e.g., `return list(self._results)`), or use a thread-safe `queue.Queue` for results.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: _stop flag lacks memory synchronization, causing workers to hang or miss shutdown
DESCRIPTION: The `_stop` boolean is written by `shutdown()` on one thread and read by worker threads in a tight loop without any synchronization primitive. On relaxed-memory architectures or with compiler/JIT optimizations, worker threads may never observe the updated value, causing them to spin indefinitely. On free-threaded CPython 3.13+ this is a formal data race. Additionally, even when the flag is eventually visible, the 1-second `queue.get(timeout=1.0)` can delay shutdown by up to one second per worker.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace `self._stop` with a `threading.Event` and use `event.set()` / `event.is_set()` for reliable inter-thread signaling.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: Unbounded queue.Queue causes memory exhaustion
DESCRIPTION: The `queue.Queue` constructor is called with no `maxsize` parameter, defaulting to unlimited size. If `submit()` is called faster than workers process jobs, the queue will grow indefinitely until system memory is exhausted and the process crashes.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Pass a `maxsize` parameter to `queue.Queue(maxsize=...)` to enforce backpressure and prevent unbounded memory growth.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: memory
TITLE: Unbounded _results list causes memory leak in long-running pools
DESCRIPTION: The `_results` list stores the outcome of every job indefinitely with no mechanism to clear or limit its size. In long-running applications, this will eventually exhaust system memory as the list grows proportional to the total number of tasks processed. Unlike the queue, results are never consumed or discarded.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement a method to clear results (e.g., `clear_results()`), provide a bounded results buffer, or use a `queue.Queue` for results so they can be consumed and removed.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: num_workers=0 or negative silently creates broken pool with silent job loss
DESCRIPTION: If `num_workers` is initialized with 0 or a negative integer, the pool starts no threads. The `submit()` method continues to accept jobs, but they accumulate in the queue forever without being processed. No error or warning is raised, making the misconfiguration silent and extremely difficult to diagnose.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Validate that `num_workers >= 1` in `__init__` and raise a `ValueError` with a descriptive message if the condition is violated.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: shutdown() raises RuntimeError on repeated calls, crashing the application
DESCRIPTION: Calling `shutdown()` multiple times triggers `w.join()` on already-joined threads, which raises a `RuntimeError` in Python. This crashes the application if shutdown is called redundantly (e.g., in exception handlers, cleanup routines, or defensive coding patterns).
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add a guard flag (e.g., `self._shutdown_called`) to prevent re-entry, or catch and suppress `RuntimeError` during join.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Shutdown does not drain the job queue, silently discarding pending work
DESCRIPTION: The `shutdown()` method sets `_stop = True` and joins workers, but does not wait for or process items remaining in the queue. Workers exit as soon as `_stop` is `True`, regardless of pending jobs. Additionally, the 1-second `queue.get(timeout=1.0)` can delay workers from noticing the stop flag. Submitted work may be silently discarded without any indication to the caller.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a "poison pill" (sentinel value) pattern: put `None` into the queue for each worker to signal a clean exit after processing all pending tasks. Alternatively, call `self._queue.join()` before returning from `shutdown()` if you want to guarantee all submitted work completes.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: data
TITLE: get_results returns direct reference to mutable internal list, violating encapsulation
DESCRIPTION: The `get_results()` method returns a direct reference to the internal `self._results` list instead of a copy. Callers can mutate the pool's internal state (e.g., `clear()`, `pop()`, insert foreign entries), and concurrent modifications by workers become visible mid-iteration for the caller, introducing subtle bugs and violating encapsulation.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Return a shallow copy of the list (e.g., `return list(self._results)`) or a snapshot taken under a lock to prevent external mutation.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: task_done() never called on queue, preventing proper synchronization
DESCRIPTION: The worker loop calls `queue.get()` but never calls `self._queue.task_done()` after processing an item. This makes it impossible for external callers to use `self._queue.join()` to block until all currently submitted tasks have been processed. If this pool design is enhanced to support graceful shutdown, `join()` will block forever because the internal unfinished-task counter never decrements.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Add `self._queue.task_done()` in a `finally` block within the worker loop's task processing logic to ensure it is called even if an exception occurs.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: fn.__name__ access fails for lambdas, callables, and built-ins, crashing workers
DESCRIPTION: Results are labeled using `fn.__name__`, which fails for lambdas (they all share the name `<lambda>`, making results indistinguishable), `functools.partial` objects, callable class instances with `__call__`, and built-in functions. An `AttributeError` will crash the worker thread and silently stop it from processing further jobs.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `getattr(fn, '__name__', repr(fn))` or similar to safely obtain a label for any callable, or better yet, return a unique job ID from `submit()` to identify results reliably.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Jobs submitted after shutdown() are silently lost and never executed
DESCRIPTION: The `submit()` method does not check the `_stop` flag before accepting new jobs. This allows users to enqueue tasks after `shutdown()` has been called. Since all workers have already exited, these jobs will never be executed, and the caller receives no error or indication that the work was discarded.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Check `self._stop` in `submit()` and raise a `RuntimeError("pool is shut down")` if true to fail fast and inform the caller.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: Exception handling obscures error details, stack traces, and exception types
DESCRIPTION: When a job raises an exception, the worker catches it and stores a string `"ERROR: {e}"` in the results list alongside successful outcomes. This discards the original exception type, stack trace, and any structured data within the exception. Additionally, a successful job could also return a string starting with "ERROR:", making results indistinguishable. Stack traces are lost entirely, making remote debugging nearly impossible. No logging occurs.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Store exceptions as distinct objects or a dedicated error type (e.g., a dataclass with the traceback), use `logging.exception()` to record the full traceback, or adopt a `concurrent.futures`-style `Future` interface that preserves the exception object.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Daemon threads risk abrupt termination without resource cleanup
DESCRIPTION: Workers are created with `daemon=True`. If the main thread exits without calling `shutdown()`, these threads are killed abruptly, potentially leaving file handles open, database connections uncommitted, transactions incomplete, or partial writes on disk. This is especially dangerous in long-running servers or applications with critical I/O.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use non-daemon threads and ensure proper cleanup via `shutdown()`, or implement a context manager (`__enter__` / `__exit__`) to guarantee shutdown on exit.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: performance
TITLE: Fixed 1-second timeout in worker loop delays graceful shutdown
DESCRIPTION: The `queue.get(timeout=1.0)` call forces workers to wait up to one second before checking the `_stop` flag. If the queue is empty and shutdown is called, each of N workers will wait up to 1 second before exiting, leading to a total shutdown latency of up to 1 second per worker. This can make shutdown sluggish and unresponsive.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a shorter timeout (e.g., `queue.get(timeout=0.1)`) or replace the polling flag with a sentinel value in the queue to trigger immediate exit.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Pool cannot be restarted after shutdown and lacks context manager support
DESCRIPTION: Once `shutdown()` is called, the pool is permanently dead — threads are joined, `_stop` is `True`, and the queue is not reset. Attempting to submit new jobs after shutdown will either fail silently or cause unexpected behavior. The class also lacks `__enter__` / `__exit__` support, so it cannot be used with `with` statements for automatic cleanup, making resource leaks likely if the caller forgets to call `shutdown()`.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement `__enter__` and `__exit__` to support the context-manager protocol, ensuring automatic cleanup. Alternatively, allow the pool to be reset or recreated after shutdown.

---END---

findings.title: Exception handling obscures error details, stack traces, and exception types
findings.description: When a job raises an exception, the worker catches it and stores a string `"ERROR: {e}"` in the results list alongside successful outcomes. This discards the original exception type, stack trace, and any structured data within the exception. Additionally, a successful job could also return a string starting with "ERROR:", making results indistinguishable. Stack traces are lost entirely, making remote debugging nearly impossible. No logging occurs.

findings.title: Daemon threads risk abrupt termination without resource cleanup
findings.description: Workers are created with `daemon=True`. If the main thread exits without calling `shutdown()`, these threads are killed abruptly, potentially leaving file handles open, database connections uncommitted, transactions incomplete, or partial writes on disk. This is especially dangerous in long-running servers or applications with critical I/O.

findings.title: Fixed 1-second timeout in worker loop delays graceful shutdown
findings.description: The `queue.get(timeout=1.0)` call forces workers to wait up to one second before checking the `_stop` flag. If the queue is empty and shutdown is called, each of N workers will wait up to 1 second before exiting, leading to a total shutdown latency of up to 1 second per worker. This can make shutdown sluggish and unresponsive.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a shorter timeout (e.g., `queue.get(timeout=0.1)`) or replace the polling flag with a sentinel value in the queue to trigger immediate exit.

findings.title: Pool cannot be restarted after shutdown and lacks context manager support
findings.description: Once `shutdown()` is called, the pool is permanently dead — threads are joined, `_stop` is `True`, and the queue is not reset. Attempting to submit new jobs after shutdown will either fail silently or cause unexpected behavior. The class also lacks `__enter__` / `__exit__` support, so it cannot be used with `with` statements for automatic cleanup, making resource leaks likely if the caller forgets to call `shutdown()`.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement `__enter__` and `__exit__` to support the context-manager protocol, ensuring automatic cleanup. Alternatively, allow the pool to be reset or recreated after shutdown.

TITLE: Unprotected shared `_stop` flag causes race conditions

SUGGESTED_FIX: Replace `_stop` with a `threading.Event` and use `event.is_set()` and `event.set()` for thread-safe signaling.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: memory

DESCRIPTION: `queue.Queue()` defaults to an unbounded size. Combined with the lack of backpressure mechanisms, rapid job submission can consume all available memory.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `get_results` exposes internal mutable state
DESCRIPTION: Returning `self._results` directly allows external code to mutate the list concurrently with worker threads, leading to race conditions and data corruption.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Return a shallow copy (`list(self._results)`) or use a thread-safe result collection mechanism with proper locking.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `shutdown` abandons queued jobs and lacks proper signaling
DESCRIPTION: Setting `_stop = True` does not unblock workers waiting on `queue.get()`. Workers will only exit after the 1-second timeout, and any jobs remaining in the queue are silently discarded.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `queue.join()` or put sentinel values (e.g., `None`) into the queue to unblock workers, and drain/process remaining jobs before exiting.

SEVERITY: medium

TITLE: `fn.__name__` fails for lambdas and builtins

SEVERITY: low

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Daemon threads cause abrupt termination on main exit
DESCRIPTION: Threads are created with `daemon=True`, meaning they will be forcefully killed if the main thread exits. This can leave results uncollected, files unclosed, or connections dangling.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Unsynchronized write to shared `_results` list from multiple threads
DESCRIPTION: Multiple worker threads call `self._results.append(...)` concurrently without any lock. Although CPython's GIL makes individual `append` calls atomic in practice, this is an implementation detail that cannot be relied upon, and the guarantee does not extend to PyPy or other runtimes. More importantly, any caller reading `_results` while workers are appending can observe a torn or incomplete view of the list. This is a data race by definition.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Protect all accesses to `_results` with a `threading.Lock`, or replace the list with a `queue.Queue` dedicated to results.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: critical
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: Non-atomic read of `_stop` flag causes workers to miss shutdown signal
DESCRIPTION: `_stop` is a plain Python `bool` written by `shutdown()` on the main thread and read by each worker thread in a tight loop without any memory barrier or lock. Although CPython's GIL makes the individual read/write atomic, the flag is checked only at the top of the loop; a worker that is blocked inside `_queue.get(timeout=1.0)` will not wake up immediately — it will keep sleeping for up to one second per cycle after `_stop` is set. Additionally, `shutdown()` sets `_stop = True` before draining the queue, so items already enqueued will never be processed.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use a `threading.Event` for the stop signal; call `event.set()` in `shutdown()` and check `event.is_set()` in the worker loop. Also join only after the queue is drained.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `shutdown()` joins workers before queue is drained
DESCRIPTION: `shutdown()` sets `_stop = True` and immediately calls `w.join()` on every worker. Any jobs still sitting in `_queue` at that moment will be silently discarded — workers check `_stop` at the top of their loop and exit on the next iteration without processing remaining items. Callers have no way to know that submitted work was dropped.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Before setting `_stop`, call `self._queue.join()` (which requires `task_done()` after each job) to drain all pending jobs, or send a sentinel value per worker to signal a clean shutdown.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: Workers silently exit on `AttributeError` when callable has no `__name__`
DESCRIPTION: `fn.__name__` is accessed unconditionally in both the success and error paths. Callables that are `functools.partial` objects, lambda wrappers returned by decorators, or instances of classes implementing `__call__` may not have a `__name__` attribute (or have a misleading one). This raises `AttributeError` inside the `except Exception` handler, which then itself raises, killing the worker thread silently with no log output.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use `getattr(fn, '__name__', repr(fn))` to safely retrieve a display name.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: observability
TITLE: Worker thread death is completely silent and undetected
DESCRIPTION: If the `AttributeError` on `fn.__name__` (or any other unexpected exception outside the inner `try/except`) kills a worker thread, the pool continues to operate with fewer workers and the caller has no way to detect this. `submit()` will keep enqueuing jobs that will never be processed if all workers die, leading to an unbounded queue growth.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Wrap the entire `_worker_loop` body in an outer `try/except BaseException` that logs the crash and optionally restarts the thread or sets an error flag accessible via a public API.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: high
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: `shutdown()` hangs forever if a job never returns
DESCRIPTION: `w.join()` with no timeout blocks indefinitely. If any submitted job hangs (network call, deadlock, infinite loop), `shutdown()` will never return, making graceful termination impossible.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Pass a `timeout` argument to `w.join()` and check `w.is_alive()` afterwards to report threads that failed to stop.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `submit()` succeeds after `shutdown()` without raising
DESCRIPTION: After `shutdown()` is called and workers have exited, calling `submit()` enqueues new jobs onto `_queue` that will never be consumed. The caller receives no indication that the pool is shut down, so jobs are silently dropped.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Check `self._stop` at the start of `submit()` and raise `RuntimeError("WorkerPool is shut down")` if it is set.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: logic
TITLE: `get_results()` returns internal mutable list by reference
DESCRIPTION: `get_results()` returns the actual `_results` list, not a copy. A caller that modifies the returned list (e.g., `results.clear()` or `results.pop()`) will corrupt the pool's internal state. Concurrent appends by workers while the caller iterates the returned list can also raise `RuntimeError: list changed size during iteration`.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Return `list(self._results)` (a snapshot copy) inside a lock so the caller gets a stable, isolated view.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: edge-case
TITLE: `num_workers=0` or negative values silently create an empty pool
DESCRIPTION: No validation is performed on `num_workers`. Passing `0` or a negative integer results in a pool with no workers; all submitted jobs queue up forever and `shutdown()` returns immediately. This is a silent misconfiguration with no diagnostic.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Raise `ValueError` at the top of `__init__` if `num_workers < 1`.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: concurrency
TITLE: `shutdown()` is not idempotent and not thread-safe
DESCRIPTION: If `shutdown()` is called from two threads concurrently, both will set `_stop = True` and both will attempt to `join()` the same worker threads. `join()` on an already-joined thread raises `RuntimeError` in Python. There is also no guard against calling `shutdown()` twice from the same thread.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Protect `shutdown()` with a lock and add a boolean flag `_shutdown_called` that prevents re-entry.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: medium
CATEGORY: design
TITLE: No way to associate a result with a specific submitted job
DESCRIPTION: Results are stored keyed only by `fn.__name__`, which is non-unique. If the same function is submitted multiple times, results are indistinguishable. There is no job ID, no future/promise, and no callback mechanism, making it impossible to correlate inputs with outputs.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Return a unique `Future`-like object from `submit()` that is resolved by the worker when the job completes, or at minimum assign each submission a unique ID.

---FINDING---
SEVERITY: low
CATEGORY: observability

DESCRIPTION: Job exceptions are caught and stored as `f"ERROR: {e}"` strings, discarding the traceback, exception type, and all structured information. Callers cannot distinguish an error result from a job that legitimately returned a string starting with "ERROR:".
SUGGESTED_FIX: Store the original exception object (or a `(exc_type, exc_value, traceback)` tuple) rather than a formatted string, or use a dedicated result wrapper type with a `success: bool` field.

---FINDING---

CATEGORY: design
TITLE: Daemon threads prevent clean process shutdown signalling
DESCRIPTION: Worker threads are created with `daemon=True`, meaning the Python interpreter will kill them abruptly when the main thread exits, without waiting for in-progress jobs to complete or for any finally blocks inside jobs to run. This can cause data corruption or partial writes if jobs perform I/O.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Use non-daemon threads and ensure `shutdown()` is always called (e.g., by implementing `__enter__`/`__exit__` to use the pool as a context manager).

---FINDING---

CATEGORY: design
TITLE: No context manager support prevents guaranteed cleanup
DESCRIPTION: There is no `__enter__`/`__exit__` implementation, so the pool cannot be used with `with` statements. Users who forget to call `shutdown()` will leak threads (non-daemon) or lose work (daemon) with no safety net.
SUGGESTED_FIX: Implement `__enter__` returning `self` and `__exit__` calling `self.shutdown()`.

---END---

findings.title: Non-atomic read of `_stop` flag causes workers to miss shutdown signal
findings.description: `_stop` is a plain Python `bool` written by `shutdown()` on the main thread and read by each worker thread in a tight loop without any memory barrier or lock. Although CPython's GIL makes the individual read/write atomic, the flag is checked only at the top of the loop; a worker that is blocked inside `_queue.get(timeout=1.0)` will not wake up immediately — it will keep sleeping for up to one second per cycle after `_stop` is set. Additionally, `shutdown()` sets `_stop = True` before draining the queue, so items already enqueued will never be processed.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a `threading.Event` for the stop signal; call `event.set()` in `shutdown()` and check `event.is_set()` in the worker loop. Also join only after the queue is drained.

findings.title: `shutdown()` joins workers before queue is drained
findings.description: `shutdown()` sets `_stop = True` and immediately calls `w.join()` on every worker. Any jobs still sitting in `_queue` at that moment will be silently discarded — workers check `_stop` at the top of their loop and exit on the next iteration without processing remaining items. Callers have no way to know that submitted work was dropped.
findings.suggested_fix: Before setting `_stop`, call `self._queue.join()` (which requires `task_done()` after each job) to drain all pending jobs, or send a sentinel value per worker to signal a clean shutdown.

findings.title: Workers silently exit on `AttributeError` when callable has no `__name__`
findings.description: `fn.__name__` is accessed unconditionally in both the success and error paths. Callables that are `functools.partial` objects, lambda wrappers returned by decorators, or instances of classes implementing `__call__` may not have a `__name__` attribute (or have a misleading one). This raises `AttributeError` inside the `except Exception` handler, which then itself raises, killing the worker thread silently with no log output.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `getattr(fn, '__name__', repr(fn))` to safely retrieve a display name.

findings.title: Worker thread death is completely silent and undetected
findings.description: If the `AttributeError` on `fn.__name__` (or any other unexpected exception outside the inner `try/except`) kills a worker thread, the pool continues to operate with fewer workers and the caller has no way to detect this. `submit()` will keep enqueuing jobs that will never be processed if all workers die, leading to an unbounded queue growth.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the entire `_worker_loop` body in an outer `try/except BaseException` that logs the crash and optionally restarts the thread or sets an error flag accessible via a public API.

findings.title: `shutdown()` hangs forever if a job never returns
findings.description: `w.join()` with no timeout blocks indefinitely. If any submitted job hangs (network call, deadlock, infinite loop), `shutdown()` will never return, making graceful termination impossible.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass a `timeout` argument to `w.join()` and check `w.is_alive()` afterwards to report threads that failed to stop.

findings.title: `submit()` succeeds after `shutdown()` without raising

findings.suggested_fix: Check `self._stop` at the start of `submit()` and raise `RuntimeError("WorkerPool is shut down")` if it is set.

findings.title: `get_results()` returns internal mutable list by reference
findings.description: `get_results()` returns the actual `_results` list, not a copy. A caller that modifies the returned list (e.g., `results.clear()` or `results.pop()`) will corrupt the pool's internal state. Concurrent appends by workers while the caller iterates the returned list can also raise `RuntimeError: list changed size during iteration`.
findings.suggested_fix: Return `list(self._results)` (a snapshot copy) inside a lock so the caller gets a stable, isolated view.

findings.title: `num_workers=0` or negative values silently create an empty pool
findings.description: No validation is performed on `num_workers`. Passing `0` or a negative integer results in a pool with no workers; all submitted jobs queue up forever and `shutdown()` returns immediately. This is a silent misconfiguration with no diagnostic.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise `ValueError` at the top of `__init__` if `num_workers < 1`.

findings.title: `shutdown()` is not idempotent and not thread-safe
findings.description: If `shutdown()` is called from two threads concurrently, both will set `_stop = True` and both will attempt to `join()` the same worker threads. `join()` on an already-joined thread raises `RuntimeError` in Python. There is also no guard against calling `shutdown()` twice from the same thread.
findings.suggested_fix: Protect `shutdown()` with a lock and add a boolean flag `_shutdown_called` that prevents re-entry.

findings.title: No way to associate a result with a specific submitted job
findings.description: Results are stored keyed only by `fn.__name__`, which is non-unique. If the same function is submitted multiple times, results are indistinguishable. There is no job ID, no future/promise, and no callback mechanism, making it impossible to correlate inputs with outputs.
findings.suggested_fix: Return a unique `Future`-like object from `submit()` that is resolved by the worker when the job completes, or at minimum assign each submission a unique ID.

findings.title: Exceptions in jobs are swallowed and stored as strings
findings.description: Job exceptions are caught and stored as `f"ERROR: {e}"` strings, discarding the traceback, exception type, and all structured information. Callers cannot distinguish an error result from a job that legitimately returned a string starting with "ERROR:".
findings.suggested_fix: Store the original exception object (or a `(exc_type, exc_value, traceback)` tuple) rather than a formatted string, or use a dedicated result wrapper type with a `success: bool` field.

findings.title: Daemon threads prevent clean process shutdown signalling
findings.description: Worker threads are created with `daemon=True`, meaning the Python interpreter will kill them abruptly when the main thread exits, without waiting for in-progress jobs to complete or for any finally blocks inside jobs to run. This can cause data corruption or partial writes if jobs perform I/O.
findings.suggested_fix: Use non-daemon threads and ensure `shutdown()` is always called (e.g., by implementing `__enter__`/`__exit__` to use the pool as a context manager).

findings.title: No context manager support prevents guaranteed cleanup
findings.description: There is no `__enter__`/`__exit__` implementation, so the pool cannot be used with `with` statements. Users who forget to call `shutdown()` will leak threads (non-daemon) or lose work (daemon) with no safety net.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement `__enter__` returning `self` and `__exit__` calling `self.shutdown()`.
